title: Negotiating with the Angolan Coast: Recreational Fishing in Colonial Luanda (1945–1975)
abstract: This article contributes to and expands the environmental history of recreational fishing through examining the development of recreational fishing in late colonial Luanda, Angola, 1945–1975. It draws on colonial archives, newspapers, tourism magazines, specialised fishing periodicals and oral testimonies to argue that recreational fishing developed through processes of dwelling in different coastal environments as practitioners and practices took shape in relation to their ecological conditions and possibilities. On the more accessible northern coast of Luanda, fishing was closely intertwined with everyday leisure, sociability and food provisioning, while the more environmentally heterogeneous southern coast demanded greater mobility and more specialised forms of angling. In the absence of systematic scientific research on marine ecosystems, recreational fishing relied on understandings of coastal dynamics and drew upon multiple layers of local knowledge. By foregrounding the changing relationships between recreational fishing, coastal environments and ecological processes, the article also contributes to broader discussions of human–environment interactions, tourism and coastal leisure.

title: Imagining Japanese Technofutures – The Role of Futurology and Science Fiction in Shaping the Information Society
abstract: The original roots of the information society (jōhō shakai) are clearly Japanese and date back to the year 1963. The concept was developed in the context of a private study group circle spearheaded by the anthropologist Umesao Tadao, including members like the science fiction writer Komatsu Sakyō and the futurologist Hayashi Yūjirō. Drawing on the methodology of science and technology studies (STS), I will show how the ideological narrative underlying Umesao’s original theory on the information industries was condensed into a sociotechnical imaginary (STI) in the years from 1963 to the end of the 1970s. This article explains why the narrative was so successful and how the Expo 1970 in Osaka served as a showcase for the public performance and stabilization of the STI. The article argues that this contributed to its lasting impact on the way in which Japanese technofutures were imagined, based on the premise of a techno-centered society.

title: Fine-tuning ASR for corpus linguistics: Singapore English
abstract: Abstract Automatic speech recognition (ASR) is increasingly used to build large spoken-language corpora, yet its role is often treated as a purely technical preprocessing step. This paper argues that ASR configuration, especially model fine-tuning, constitutes a form of corpus design that directly shapes what linguistic analyses such resources can support. Focusing on Singapore English, we fine-tune six OpenAI Whisper model sizes on conversational data from Part 3 of Singapore’s National Speech Corpus and evaluate sixteen ASR systems, including baseline Whisper models and two alternative architectures, using word and character error rates on two held-out test sets. The best-performing fine-tuned model is then used to generate YCSEP_v2, an updated version of the YouTube Corpus of Singapore English Podcasts (approximately 620 h of audio). Evaluation goes beyond aggregate accuracy to examine linguistically salient phenomena. We compare corpus-level frequencies of discourse particles and disfluency markers and analyse three morphosyntactic variables (third-person singular -s, past tense zero marking, and copula absence). Fine-tuning yields substantial gains in transcription accuracy while improving the recovery of interactional features and reducing normalization towards mainstream English morphosyntax. The resulting transcripts diverge in systematic ways, demonstrating that ASR choices influence not only transcript quality but also corpus-based generalizations about linguistic …

title: “I Was Bewitched by an Ant”: A Cosmo‐Ecological Perspective on Human‐Ant Relationships in Indigenous Peruvian Amazonia
abstract: ABSTRACT This article employs a dialogue‐based framework that draws on anthropology, ethnobiology and ecology to explore the multifaceted relationship between the Asháninka people of the Peruvian Amazonia and a group of insects they recognize as ants. Ants play a significant role in terrestrial ecosystems, acting as powerful agents of landscape recycling and transformation. They are viewed ambivalently in various human cultures: being admired for their organizational skills and work yet also blamed for significant agricultural losses. For Amazonian indigenous groups, however, ants are more than just “an ecological force” or “love‐or‐hate” creatures. This article examines how ecological reasoning and moral reasoning are mutually constitutive in shaping the agency with which the Asháninka people endow “ants”. Twenty six names of ethnospecies of “ants” were recorded for which scientific correspondence was established based on the collected specimens. The ethnoclassification of ants falls into two major categories: The type of environment they inhabit and the level of harm they produce. In cosmological animistic terms, some “ants” are attributed with a predatory nature to bewitch and induce illness in people. We conclude that the attribution of harmful faculties to “ants” does not result from ecological reasoning being influenced by moral reasoning, nor vice versa. Rather, ecological observation and moral interpretation are mutually constitutive: the habits and behavior of …

title: Tracing affective change: topic modeling and emotional semantics of gender in eighteenth-century British fiction
abstract: Abstract This article re-examines the changing forms of emotional expression in eighteenth-century British fiction by combining topic modeling with semantic and literary-historical analysis. Scholarship on sentimental and Gothic fiction has long emphasized the importance of tears, sensibility, and heightened affect, yet it remains difficult to determine how such affective vocabularies are distributed across a broader corpus without beginning from a fixed list of preselected emotional terms. For this reason, the study begins with Latent Dirichlet Allocation as an exploratory procedure for mapping recurrent lexical fields in a corpus of seventy-nine novels published between 1719 and 1796. One prominent topic brings together words such as cry, mind, heart, father, answer, and return, suggesting a field of emotional, familial, and interpersonal expression. The discussion then uses the word cry as a point of entry into this affective field, whose eighteenth-century uses range from tearful affect to vocal exclamation and formulaic speech attribution. By combining topic modeling, context-based semantic classification, normalized frequency analysis, gender-based comparison, and a supplementary chunk-level check, the study shows that weeping-related affect becomes especially prominent in female-authored fiction of the late eighteenth century, while mid-century male-authored fiction displays a more limited and historically distinct concentration of sentimental expression.

title: Transimperial Manhood: Theodore Roosevelt and Gendered Politics in US-Japanese Relations
abstract: The gender ideology of no other US president has elicited as much scholarly fascination as that of Theodore Roosevelt. Historians have closely analyzed his transformation from sickly child to big stick-wielding outdoorsman, highlighting how his overbearing father, frontier experience, and the societal transformations of the Gilded Age shaped an idiosyncratic gendered worldview that guided his political decisions.1 Neil Cogan even argues that manhood was Roosevelt’s central political organizing principle, linking progressivism and global power concerns over civilizational struggle within a common gendered vision.2 So far, this literature has treated this vision as a domestic construct rooted in US socialization and projected outward through political actions. Such a reading overlooks the realities of the United States in which Roosevelt came into political maturity: an ascending empire embedded in global networks of shared imperial knowledge, culture, and practice. An avid reader and passionate traveler, Roosevelt actively and enthusiastically participated in this global system. How did it impact his gendered formation? What does this tell us about the role of gendered knowledge circulation in shaping imperial diplomatic culture?

title: Financing Water Services through Ottoman Cash Waqfs in Rumelia
abstract: This article examines how cash waqfs financed water services in Ottoman Rumelia (the empire’s Balkan provinces) from the sixteenth to the early twentieth century, as a contribution to both waqf studies and environmental history. It draws on a primary-source database of 953 Rumelian endowment records, from which 165 cash waqfs linked to water provision were identified and analysed. It makes three arguments. First, these foundations formed a significant, regionally differentiated mechanism of public provision: they supported fountains and waterways above all, but also bridges, sebils and mixed service clusters. Second, their importance lay less in establishing water services than in sustaining them: by converting preserved capital into recurring income for maintenance, wages and repair, cash waqfs operated as an institutionalised mechanism of sustainability. Third, the geography of this provision followed the environmental and urban structure of the Balkans, so that mountain, riverine and port settings produced distinct service profiles.

title: From Eradication to Adaptation: The Colorado Potato Beetle in Cold War Czechoslovakia
abstract: This article examines the Colorado potato beetle in postwar Czechoslovakia as a case through which to explore the relationship between environmental processes and socialist environmental governance. While the beetle was widely framed in Cold War propaganda as an ‘American’ agent of sabotage, the paper argues that its political significance cannot be reduced to ideological projection. Rather, it emerged from the interaction between the insect’s biological characteristics and the state’s efforts to monitor, control, and eradicate it. Drawing on archival sources from agricultural and party institutions, the analysis traces how the spread of the beetle in the early 1950s was transformed from an agronomic problem into an issue of political urgency and security. It shows how systems of monitoring and mapping, mass mobilisation campaigns, and large-scale chemical interventions were deployed in response, while the beetle’s capacity for rapid reproduction and repeated re-infestation continually exposed the limits of these strategies. Conceptually, the article engages with recent work in environmental history and more-than-human approaches to examine how nonhuman life can shape perception, political interpretation, and practices of governance. From this perspective, the Colorado potato beetle can be understood not only as an object of discourse but as a persistent ecological presence that influenced both the practices and expectations of state intervention. The article further shows …

title: The First World War and Japan’s cabinet system: how the conflict changed the perception and reception of foreign constitutional models by Japanese elites (1912–1920)
abstract: The modern Japanese state, built on the Meiji Constitution (1889–1947), has long been understood as inspired by a Prussian model. Recent historiography, however, emphasises a paradigm shift in Japanese national identity after the First World War and the development of party politics in the 1920s. How did the experience of this conflict alter the vision of European constitutional frameworks and the choice of foreign models for interpreting Japan’s own political institutions? This article, while focusing on the cabinet system, addresses this question by analysing constitutional commentaries and reform projects by scholars, statesmen, and journalists across three chronological stages. First, it shows that doctrinal debates from 1912 to 1914 were polarised by ideologies favouring the German or British models. Second, it observes essential changes in information pipelines during the war, a detachment from Germany, and increasing praise for Britain’s resilience. Third, it argues that reform projects by influential actors in the war’s immediate aftermath were designed after the United Kingdom’s recent institutional evolutions. These considerations shed light on an early stage of the global dissemination of the Westminster model and suggest its influence went beyond the Dominions and the post-Second World War Commonwealth.

title: Torii Ryūzō’s anthropometric measurements and photography in colonial Korea
abstract: Several historians have analyzed anthropologist Torii Ryuzō's ethnographic research across East Asia and the Pacific, including his use of photography in conducting fieldwork. However, scholars have largely overlooked his interest in physical anthropology in the early part of his career. This article investigates Torii's anthropometric research in Korea during the 1910s to show that, despite a large amount of data collected through years of fieldwork, institutional and technical reasons prevented his research from being part of the scholarly dialogue in the following years. Torii was seeking to combine anthropometric measurements with photography to innovate a research method that would critically engage contemporary European anthropological scholarship, through the combination of qualitative and quantitative approaches. However, from the 1920s, physical anthropology in Japan underwent a major shift with the widespread adoption of Rudolf Martin's anthropometric methods. With Keijō Imperial University in colonial Korea serving as one of the important research hubs, anatomists emphasizing precise measurements and statistical analysis dominated Japanese physical anthropology. Consequently, despite its scale and the attempt to arrive at an innovative methodology, Torii never managed to publish his anthropometry data or anthropometric photographs from Korea. This article thus shows, through tracing the disappearance of Torii's physical anthropology from academic discourse, …
journal: East Asian Science, Technology and Society

title: Following East African cowries: Currency supply, transoceanic exchange, and monetary transformation in the nineteenth century
abstract: Abstract This article recentres East Africa in the global history of cowrie shells by tracing the trajectories of Monetaria annulus —the East African cowrie species—across interconnected monetary arenas in the nineteenth century. Situating African monetary history within transoceanic processes, it argues that the ‘great cowrie inflation’ in West Africa was closely tied to the reorganization of procurement networks, labour regimes, and commercial infrastructures in the Western Indian Ocean. Viewed from Zanzibar, the massive export of East African cowries emerges as the outcome of intersecting processes: price fluctuations in Maldivian shells, the expansion of the palm oil trade, extractive labour networks, and imperial interests. The article further shows that the same infrastructures were later reoriented toward the Great Lakes region, tracing how a single commodity connected East and West Africa, the Indian Ocean, and the Atlantic world. Following cowries across these overlapping spaces demonstrates that monetary history—wherever it is written—cannot be fully understood without attending to the supply-side infrastructures that made money available.

title: Regionalising development: UN expertise and the making of a pan-Arab welfare field, 1949–59
abstract: Abstract In August 1949, the first Social Research Seminar for the Arab States convened in Beirut; five further seminars followed over the next decade. Drawing on Arabic-language seminar proceedings and UN archival records, this article recovers these largely overlooked gatherings to analyse how a distinct regional developmental field took shape in the post-war Arab East. UN institutional uncertainty in the late 1940s allowed the Arab League to capture this format, to authenticate global development through civilisational framing—most visibly in a lexical shift from emancipatory inʿāsh (reinvigoration) to custodial riʿāya (guardianship)—and to consolidate a self-sustaining professional field. The resulting regional arena mediated between global circulation and national implementation while proving durably compatible with the authoritarian welfare regimes emerging across the region.

title: AI lexicography and literary texts: applying Gricean maxims to evaluate ChatGPT’s performance on Shakespearean vocabulary
abstract: Abstract This study evaluates the reliability of ChatGPT-3.5, accessed via its 2024 public web interface, in identifying and contextualizing Shakespearean lexical items within Elizabethan English. Using five lexical items (bread, blood, grace, honest, and wit) as test cases, ChatGPT’s outputs are systematically compared with established reference resources, including Shakespeare’s Words and the Shakespeare Complete Works. The analysis adopts Grice’s cooperative principle—Quality, Quantity, Relevance, and Manner—as an evaluative framework for assessing the accuracy, proportionality, relevance, and clarity of artificial intelligence (AI)-generated responses. A total of eighty responses were independently coded by six raters, yielding perfect inter-rater agreement (Fleiss’ κ = 1.00). Results show that violations of the maxim of Quality—particularly factual inaccuracies, misattribution, and fabricated citations—were dominant across all lexical items, despite variation in semantic domain. While ChatGPT demonstrates fluency and occasional contextual sensitivity, its outputs exhibit instability and limited reliability in historically grounded literary tasks. The findings, specific to ChatGPT-3.5, suggest that this model generation may function as a supplementary tool for exploratory or pedagogical purposes but cannot replace curated lexicographic resources in Shakespearean scholarship; whether these limitations persist in more recent model generations remains an open question for …

title: Multispecies Affectivity in Albrecht Dürer's Material Renaissance
abstract: This chapter situates Dürer’s drawings of birds within shifting multispecies relationships in Renaissance Nuremberg to conceptualise artistic innovation as situated material knowledge, and to consider animals as key contributors to Renaissance material creativity. The chapter applies an ethno-ornithological approach and builds on the inspiring work of anthropologists, namely multispecies ethnographers who examine the everyday practices and quotidian experiences of multispecies entanglement. The chapter uncovers the extent to which everyday affective practices of bird–human relationships mattered to the world of making in Renaissance Nuremberg, focusing on cooking, healing, hunting, and stuffing, as well as their impact on Dürer’s creative practice.

title: The Questio de aqua et terra : a computational authorship verification study
abstract: Abstract The Questio de aqua et terra is a cosmological treatise traditionally attributed to Dante Alighieri. However, the authenticity of this text is controversial, due to discrepancies with Dante’s established works and to the absence of contemporary references. This study investigates the authenticity of the Questio via computational authorship verification (AV), a class of techniques that combine supervised machine learning and stylometry. We build a family of AV systems and we assemble a corpus of 330 thirteenth- and fourteenth-century Latin texts, which we use to comparatively evaluate the AV systems through leave-one-out cross-validation. Our best-performing system achieves high verification accuracy (F1=0.941) despite the heterogeneity of the corpus in terms of textual genre. The key contribution to the accuracy of this system is shown to come from Distributional Random Oversampling (DRO), a technique specially tailored to text classification, which is here used for the first time in AV. The application of the AV system to the Questio returns a highly confident prediction that Dante is indeed its author. These findings contribute to the debate on the authorship of the Questio and highlight DRO’s potential in the application of AV to cultural heritage.

title: Vibrant Maya Ruins: Community Territorialization in Ake, Yucatán, Mexico
abstract: Abstract The ruination of many Maya cities in the northern Yucatán Peninsula toward the end of the Classic period (AD 300–900) did not necessarily bring about abandonment in those spaces. On the contrary, the transformation of monumental Maya architecture to heaps of rubble fostered new relations among humans, matter, and other-than-human entities in ancestral places. This article examines the formation and dissolution of a community in Ake’s epicenter, an ancestral Maya city located in present-day Yucatán, Mexico, from approximately AD 1100 to 1550. By AD 1000, monumental buildings were transforming into ruins due to human neglect and the action of gravity, erosion, humidity, and vegetation. These ruins were vibrant entities that prompted the growth of plants, attracted animals, materialized deities and ancestors, and generated human affects, conditions that assembled community life after political collapse. This article offers a glimpse into an ancestral Maya perspective on ruins. This Indigenous perspective was relational, nonhuman centered, and conceived of ruins as lively entities in more-than-human communities.

title: Dystopia as Forecast: How the Japanese Privacy Movement Contested an Imagined Data State, 1970s–1990s
abstract: During the 1970s, as computerization became central to Japan’s public administration, the state advanced a sociotechnical imaginary of an efficient, digitally unified information society, built on integrating personal data and culminating in a proposed national identification number. In response, a social movement emerged to contest the concentration of informational power in state and corporate systems. This article argues that the movement is best understood as a politics of anticipation. It mobilized against a data state that did not yet exist, contesting the imaginary as a claim about the future, not present harms. Drawing on imported and projected examples, activists fought on two fronts, protection of personal data and access to government information, in an anticipatory contest that co-produced Japan’s data-governance regime. Tracing the movement from the 1972 founding of the Central Council for Opposing the National ID System and Protecting Privacy through census resistance and activists’ entry into local government, the article shows that the feared data state arrived only in constrained form, hedged by the oversight the movement had demanded. Neither the imaginary’s triumph nor the movement’s victory, the resulting settlement turns on the question it first raised: who should control the collection, circulation, and use of personal information?

title: Imagining a Cashless Future for Japan: Sociotechnical Imaginaries in a Consensus-Driven Society
abstract: This article examines Japan’s transition toward a cashless society through the lens of sociotechnical imaginaries, highlighting how technological and social factors interact in a consensus-driven context. The analysis focuses on six editions of the Cashless Roadmap (2019–2024) published by the semi-governmental Payments Japan Association (PJA), which brings together state, industry, and consumer perspectives. Employing content analysis, the article identifies four dominant imaginaries shaping Japan’s cashless future: seamless and invisible payments; digital infrastructure as a driver of social transformation; cashless as a new lifestyle; and inclusive, equitable digital participation for all. These imaginaries overlap and evolve in response to events such as the COVID-19 pandemic, government incentive programs, and international benchmarks, particularly China’s model of QR-based payments. Findings show that while globally circulating visions of data monetization, payment growth, and user experience resonate in Japan, they are reframed to emphasize trust, transparency, and social cohesion. The discussion highlights both synergies and tensions among the four imaginaries. Their complementarities reinforce a multi-dimensional strategy for efficiency, lifestyle transformation, and inclusion, aligned to support national renewal. Ultimately, the Cashless Roadmaps fulfill a performative role, mobilizing diverse stakeholders and embedding cashless payment within Japan’s broader …

title: Come a long way: The global historian’s craft, twenty years on
abstract: Abstract Twenty years after the founding of the Journal of Global History , this anniversary article takes stock of global history: its trajectory, its markers of disciplinary maturity, its political sense of purpose, and the difficulties and limits of the enterprise. Concerns after 2016 that global history might lose its relevance in a changing political climate have, thus far, not been borne out. By many measures, global history is both a flourishing field and an influential sensibility. Its enduring contribution, this article argues, lies in how it has helped, and continues to help, bring about a fuller, more accurate, and more complete understanding of the ever-incomplete ‘selection of facts’ that constitutes history, our humble truth. Twenty years on, global historians know their field’s limitations but also its value. They know that they have brought the world into history—and that this is no small thing.

title: Ibn Khaldûn as a Colonial Archive: Toward an Epistemic Decolonization
abstract: Abstract This article examines Ibn Khaldûn not as a stable, timeless precursor of modern social science but as a figure constituted through colonial translation and reception. Focusing on nineteenth- and twentieth-century French and English translations of the Muqaddimah , it argues that Ibn Khaldûn emerged in modern scholarship as a colonial archive—a site where translation, race, and epistemic authority intersected to produce new forms of historical and sociological knowledge. Through close comparison of Arabic originals and their European translations, the article shows how colonial epistemologies reconfigured Ibn Khaldûn’s analytical categories—particularly those concerning tribe, generation, civilization, and climate—into racialized frameworks foreign to his medieval context. It further demonstrates how this translated Ibn Khaldûn became selectively relevant to European social science while remaining excluded from its canonical genealogies. Finally, the article critically reassesses the enduring claim that Ibn Khaldûn articulated racist views about Black populations, showing that this attribution itself belongs to the colonial archive generated through translation rather than to the epistemic logic of the original text. The article thus contributes to comparative histories of knowledge, colonial epistemology, and the global formation of the social sciences.
journal: Comparative Studies in Society and History

title: True Digital Poiesis: A Conceptual Framework and Interface Design for Generative AI in the Humanities
abstract: This article introduces True Digital Poiesis (TDP), a conceptual pedagogical framework and proposed interface design for engaging generative AI in the Humanities. Drawing on experiential learning theory and grounded in the humanistic preoccupation with alterity — the otherness of history — TDP proposes the use of AI to simulate premodern events while foregrounding the active interpretive effort involved in constructing the past. The framework envisions the design of a digital prompt-builder, the Event Cruncher Stylus (ECS), and a structured critical review process, both of which are designed to support student engagement with the complexities of historical construction. In presenting the theoretical foundation, practical applications, and interface design of TDP, this article argues that precise and responsible use of AI in historical simulation — ranging from non-immersive to fully immersive simulative modes — requires a systematic, embodied method for engaging the alterity of the past. As a conceptual proposal grounded in hermeneutic theory and experiential learning research, TDP is presented here as a framework whose empirical evaluation through classroom implementation and outcome assessment is a primary objective of ongoing and future research.

title: Genealogies of protest and resistance in the Scottish Highlands and islands after 1750
abstract: Abstract Histories of protest in the Highlands and Islands have been largely limited to the study of dramatic and large-scale events driven by issues of possession of and access to land after 1850. Most research to date has tended to focus on the crofting counties of the north-west of the region and the paradigmatic land raid, with alternate forms of protest and at different times often relegated to little more than a footnote. Experiences of agrarian improvement and the dramatic economic and social transformations of the ‘first phase of clearance’ between 1750 and 1820 have meanwhile stressed the apathy of the Highlander, who passively, if reluctantly, accepted his new lot. This article provides a review and critique of the literature on Scottish protest. It concludes with some reflections on future research agendas beyond these established genealogies and calls for a return to the archives of the everyday and a focus on alternative protest repertoires beyond that of protest against clearance.

title: Borrowed Time: Sovereign Debt and Temporal Disorder In Socialist Yugoslavia
abstract: Abstract When Francis Fukuyama described the collapse of state socialism as marking the “end of history,” he captured the imagination of the post-Cold War moment, rendering the fall of the Berlin Wall a metonym for the definitive eclipse of communism and the advent of a new era of liberal capitalist hegemony. For Europe’s Left, the term became associated with a moment of profound demoralization. Fukuyama’s end of history, however, was only one moment of a longer and more expansive crisis in the socialist order of time. This crisis can be traced back to the global economic upheavals of the 1970s that impacted both social democracy in the West and state socialism in the East. A decade before crowds forced their way across a divided Berlin, socialism on both sides of the Iron Curtain had entered an existential decline. This article argues that the sovereign debt crises that beset European states in the final decade of the Cold War disrupted socialism’s regime of historicity. It develops this argument with reference to late-socialist Yugoslavia and demonstrates how the temporal conditions of sovereign indebtedness shaped popular culture. Through a reading of the films Balkanski špijun (1984) and Već viđeno (1987), the article argues that the erosion of socialism’s horizons of expectation fostered a new experience of historical time in which the past returned in uncanny, troubling, and ultimately destructive ways.
journal: Comparative Studies in Society and History

title: Toppling coloniality: interventions on tainted monuments toward an open future
abstract: The article examines how monuments tied to colonial histories can operate as instruments of the ‘colonization of the mind’, and how interventions on them can become anti-colonial practices. Drawing on decolonial theory and recent scholarship on tainted monuments, it argues that commemorations do not merely depict the past; as objects that dwell in the temporality of coloniality, they authorize present hierarchies and future-oriented commitments, often through seemingly neutral artistic forms. The paper maps distinct intervention repertoires based on Latin American cases mainly from 2020–2023, and identifies differences in approaches related to agency, temporality, and visibility. It proposes six criteria for interventions with anti-colonial force: broad participation, institutional avowal, bottom-up deliberation, multi-dimensional attention to affect and intimate attachments, enduring and dynamic visibility, and explicit display of temporal continuities between colonial violence and contemporary oppressive structures. The paper concludes that keeping intervened monuments visible – preserving their documentary condition while deactivating their monumental power – can function as an open, everyday visual debate about the past and the futures it enables.

title: Culture and Contradiction Before the End of History: From Socialist Legacies to Market Logics
abstract: Abstract In late-socialist Romania, the state sought to govern economic crisis by demanding market-like conduct from cultural institutions while continuing to bind them to the political structures of socialism. Drawing on archival planning reports, media accounts, and post-socialist recollections, this article traces the emergence of a “self-financing regime” that reorganized cultural production around revenue generation, entrepreneurial conduct, and managerial accountability. I argue that self-financing constituted neither a retreat of socialism nor an incipient transition to capitalism, but an experiment in governing crisis by relocating the burdens of economic survival onto institutions themselves. This shift generated a contradictory institutional world: cultural actors were compelled to pursue economic self-sufficiency and become self-optimizing subjects even as markets remained ideologically repudiated, socialist obligations endured, and nominal decentralization extended bureaucratic oversight. Yet contradiction did not simply signal the incoherence of late socialism. As these tensions became embedded in everyday institutional practice, contradiction provided the very means through which austerity was rendered governable. The Romanian case thus shows how market-like rationalities could emerge from within socialist crisis management and crystallize into historically distinct forms of governance. By situating these entanglements before the so-called “end of history,” the …
journal: Comparative Studies in Society and History

title: Imagineering the Future: A Mixed-Method Mapping of Japan’s Corporate Imaginaries of Metaverse Sustainability
abstract: Japanese metaverse discourse relies heavily on collective, often prescriptive visions of technoscientific futures. In general, these hyperbolic visions might be similar across the globe, but what about aspects they deliberately gloss over? Driven by this question, I examine Japan’s corporate metaverse discourse, focusing on the rarely thematized aspects of environmental and social sustainability. Based on Jasanoff’s concept of sociotechnical imaginaries, Adloff’s imaginaries of sustainability, and Brause et al.’s SIPC framework, my mixed-method approach identifies metaverse imaginaries through a combination of digital corpora analysis and semi-structured interviews with 14 expert practitioners from Japan. As a result, five sociotechnical imaginaries of sustainability emerge within Japan’s corporate metaverse discourse: anticipation, digital revolution, pragmatism, cultural essentialism, and technosolutionism. My analysis shows that the answers a nascent metaverse is expected to provide with regard to ecological and social crises depend on the type of metaverse we imagine and its relationship with the real world. The findings suggest that Japan’s imaginaries of metaverse sustainability are uniquely situated between an essentialized past, a challenging present, and distant futures, as well as between Japanese particularities and global tech ideologies.

title: Conflict, Struggle, and Detecting the Real: Newman’s Epistemology, Cognate Disciplines, and Renewing Catechesis Today
abstract: Abstract The general purpose of this article is to investigate how conflict and struggle, observed in history and experienced in one’s own being, might serve to bolster faith. Two areas are of particular significance regarding the strengthening of faith vis-à-vis conflict: facilitating assent to religious truth claims and renewing catechetical approaches. Concretely, this article is comprised of three sections. The first section briefly elucidates the terms ‘catechesis’, ‘conflict’, and ‘struggle’. The second section provides an overview of Newman’s religious epistemology and analyzes how it conceives of struggle in the process of coming to assent and certitude regarding religious truth claims, primarily treating Newman’s major 1870 work on religious epistemology, An Essay in Aid of a Grammar of Assent . The third section then analyzes how conflict and struggle are being incorporated into a variety of cognate disciplines to improve student engagement and outcomes. Case studies demonstrate the potential fruit of being forthright regarding the struggles of major figures in history, as well as the value of introducing students to manageable levels of confusion and responsibility for course content. The conclusion offers several constructive reflections while not shying away from the pitfalls that accompany any incorporation of conflict and struggle into the catechetical process.

title: Ambiguously queer: interrogating youth and queerness in Kyoto Animation’s adaptation of Sound! Euphonium
abstract: Found across a wide variety of genres, youth is a popular setting for media in Japan. Often focused on school club activities, narratives set during adolescence feature intense relationships between members of the same sex that toe the line between homoromantic and homosocial. The language used in the texts and by the creators often supports both readings, with the audience left to draw their own conclusions based on how they understand youth. While previous scholarship has looked at queerness in youth-focused texts, less has been written about how the association a text has with youth affects queer readings of the language of the texts. Through a textual and discourse analysis of the anime Sound! Euphonium (2015–2024), as well as published interviews with creators and online fan discussion about it, this article interrogates the relationship between queerness and youth in the Japanese media. I argue that youth has a normative effect in the Japanese media sphere, obfuscating the existence of queer readings by providing a normative explanation for even the queerest of language. I further suggest that Sound! Euphonium more widely reflects the ambiguity that pervades representations of queerness during female adolescence in the Japanese media.

title: The Right to Communicate: UNESCO and the politics of global communication, 1969–1987
abstract: Abstract The Right to Communicate (RtC) is the idea that individuals possess not only the freedom to ‘seek, receive and impart information’, as laid down in Article 19 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR), but also the right to communicate horizontally with their peers, using technologies new and old. The brainchild of Jean d’Arcy, a French broadcaster and official who argued in 1969 that Article 19 should be updated to reflect the new technological possibilities, the concept inspired an international effort to write the RtC into human rights law. This article examines the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization’s (UNESCO) campaign to define this new human right, showing how initial enthusiasm was undermined by a widespread conviction that collective rights were a threat to individual rights; the difficulty of squaring the Global South’s state-led vision of communication with d’Arcy’s anti-statist ideals; and the vocal opposition of Western governments and NGOs, who increasingly saw the concept as a threat to freedom of information.

title: Knowledge uprooted: Transimperial forestry and the hiring of foreign experts in the Dutch East Indies, 1920s–1930s
abstract: Abstract This article examines the global networks underpinning colonial forestry in the Dutch East Indies in the interwar period. In the aftermath of the First World War, a renewed surge towards the internationalisation of the forest sciences served to open up imperial knowledge systems to a wider pool of outside expertise. This provided opportunities for smaller, thus far underresearched parties like the Nordic states, as explored here through a case study of a group of international foresters employed by the Dutch colonial administration in the 1930s. The article combines transimperial and global history approaches into a multisite analysis of both the scholarly exchanges that led to their initial hiring and their subsequent on-the-ground work in the colony. It is argued that an actor-oriented interrogation of the practical networks and internal frictions of colonial knowledge work reveals the hesitant emergence of a multilateral system that anticipated the post-1945 regime of international development.

title: The Futuristic Imagination Sprawl: Charting Concepts vs. Social Realities
abstract: This introductory article provides the theoretical framing for the Japanese Studies special issue, ‘Japanese Technofutures – Imaginaries, Narratives, Social Realities’. The contributions focus on Japan as a primary site for technofuturistic imaginations, driven by both external techno-orientalist attributions and deeply internalized self-conceptualizations. Yet, these technological promises frequently present a paradox: they commodify the future while masking persistent social and structural inequalities in the present. Acknowledging that both area studies and science and technology studies (STS) discursively construct their respective subjects, this introduction bridges the two fields by charting the conceptual landscape of the ‘futuristic imagination sprawl’. It demonstrates that differentiating Sheila Jasanoff’s sociotechnical imaginaries from adjacent concepts enriches our investigation of future-oriented imaginations with greater clarity and precision. Grounded in this framework, the special issue’s case studies examine how Japanese technofutures are envisioned, institutionalized, translated, and contested from the 1960s to the present.

title: ‘Floating Property’: Litigating Coastal Enclosure in Belfast’s Crown Court, 1886–1887
abstract: This article examines a case brought before the Belfast Spring Assizes in 1886 and again in 1887, in which three coastal smallholders from Ballycastle, County Antrim, were prosecuted for theft of seaweed from shores claimed by a local landlord. Drawing upon a variety of documents produced from the trial, this article examines how Irish legal institutions managed the indeterminate foreshore environment during a period of considerable land law reform. Central to this investigation is the consideration of how evidentiary hierarchies, upheld in court proceedings and enshrined in public judgements, informed public challenges to coastal enclosure. Written evidence bases (maps, leases, rent books) were privileged over oral testimony, with the effect of reinforcing absolutist, totalising visions of property ownership. Yet, through the hearing of oral testimonies, the courtroom retained a crucial function as a theatre for airing popular counterclaims. These depositions complicated the prosecution’s vision of coastal ownership, articulating the foreshore as a terraqueous environment governed by local custom and informal systems of exchange that were underpinned by understandings of reciprocity and common rights rather than exclusive title.

Earthquakes in Colonial Bengal. Environmental, Social and Political Dimensions: Bengal and Assam Region, Later Nineteenth to Early Twentieth Century
abstract: This article presents a study of the environmental, social and political consequences of the devastating earthquakes that rattled the British Indian province of Bengal between 1869 and 1934. Based on four major seismic events the Cachar earthquake of 1869, the Bengal earthquake of 1885, the Great Indian Earthquake of 1897 and the Bihar-Nepal earthquake of 1934 – it examines how these natural disasters intersected with colonial rule, the production of scientific knowledge, social hierarchies and emergent nationalist politics. Based on archival sources, contemporary accounts and scientific reports, the article shows that earthquakes were moments of critical exposure of the fragility of colonial infrastructure, a stimulus to scientific investigation, a magnifier of social inequalities and a generator of spaces for colonial imposition as well as indigenous action. The findings illustrate the nature of the relationship between natural hazards and human systems under the tide of British imperialism in South Asia. This article was published open access under a CC BY 4.0 licence: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ .

title: The Digital Squid and the Digital Sewer: Bong Joon-ho’s The Host
abstract: Abstract The suggested connections between digital technology and mollusks, as well as other tentacular creatures, in Bong Joon-ho’s Gwoemul/The Host (2006), reflect historical links between the digital and the molluscan cephalopod, while also finding expression in the “cthulhoid” elements of contemporary culture. I discuss the digital aspects of South Korea’s grappling with globalized neoliberal capitalism, including its role in the derivative trading that saw so many Koreans take on unpayable debt in the aftermath of the IMF ’s supposed bailout. This globalized and digital Korea is as much the “monster” in Bong’s film as the titular creature itself, as is reflected in the “animalization” of the film’s downwardly mobile characters. The monster in The Host is not so much the enemy of the film’s protagonists as an expression of the “sewerification” and animalization of their lives, as well as of the “alien intelligence” that a cephalopod-like/“cthulhoid” digital capital possesses in the contemporary Korean world.

title: Representing Animals in Asian Screen Media: An Introduction
abstract: Abstract In Asia, the representation of animals serves as a narrative intermediary for contemplating the relationship between humans and nature. From ancient times to the present, Asian religions such as Buddhism and Japanese Shintoism have regarded animals as incarnations of deities. The mythical nature of animals is preserved in Asian screen media through adaptations based on ancient stories. In contemporary human life, animals have become production assets for labor, companions as pets, and content for digital platforms. The representation of animals not only reflects human life but also becomes critical of the ethics in the relationships between humans and animals in this late Anthropocene era. This special issue gathers scholars from across national borders to discuss how the representation of animals in East Asian screen media, including cinema, animation, gallery-based moving image, and short video platforms, differently reflects national culture, colonial history, and contemporary environmental and platform politics on screen.

title: The Contribution of Environmental History to Understanding Fires in Landscapes: Exploring Analogies between Case Studies in South Africa and Portugal
abstract: ABSTRACT This article offers comparative environmental histories of wildfires in Portugal and South Africa from c .1860 to the 2010s, using a framework derived from Elinor Ostrom’s work on managing communal environmental systems and an emerging integrated approach to wildfire management. In doing so, it sets out ideas for writing more systematic comparative historical analyses of wildfires while also using the case studies to show how historical analysis enriches case study approaches usually focused on natural and social science data and perspectives. It considers the particular versus the general, investigating whether historical analyses of fire use, management and occurrence can generate more holistic apprehensions of wildfire scenarios.

title: Burning the Black Dragon, Creating Dongbei: Fire Social Ecological History in Northeastern China, 1945–2005
abstract: ABSTRACT Modern China’s understanding of wildfires is primarily applied science aimed at resolving issues related to fire management. Dominant conceptions of fire focus on physical processes and interactions – a physical paradigm. This was not always the case and this historical survey and analysis of fires in northeast China (Dongbei) seeks to unpack a more biological and cultural wildfire paradigm based on key policy evolutions and wildfire events. Northeast China was transformed over the course of the twentieth century from mixed and boreal forest-grassland-wetland interface into one of the major ‘breadbaskets’ of China through migration, infrastructure and agricultural development, and extensive fire use and wildfire outbreaks. China’s understanding of fire, firefighting and fire policy evolved in tandem with this transformation, and increasing experience with major wildfire disasters in the region, leading to a more applied science and professionalised wildfire management approach. Based on historical analysis of settlement and landscape management trends, use of fire in land reclamation, together with evolving wildfire suppression and firefighting administrations in northeastern China, fostered a range of fire policy frameworks – from limited colonial regulation to socialist revolution and collectivisation approaches – and, overall, a total war on wildfire with varying success, through current wildfire management models.

title: The Burning Landscapes of the Serras of Southern Portugal: A Silent Transition from Fire-Centric Landscapes to Massive Forest Fires
abstract: ABSTRACT Over the course of the 1960s, the Monchique mountains in southern Portugal moved from a cereal-based rural economy to one based on eucalyptus trees channelled into the pulpwood industry. This swift change entailed the transition from a landscape mostly organised around fire farming practices to a forested landscape frequently devastated by large fires. This article proposes a long-term understanding of these changes and, more broadly, of the emergence of the current fire regime in the Portuguese mountains, focusing on the political, scientific, and ecological opposition between forest and fire that unfolded from the second half of the nineteenth century. Monchique shows, paradoxically, that rural fire use long resisted the ideal of a fire-free landscape until the birth of the recent massive forest fires.

title: Burning as a Throughline: A History of Anthropogenic Fires in the National Forests of North Carolina
abstract: ABSTRACT Anthropogenic fires constitute a throughline in the fire history of Nantahala and Pisgah National Forests of Western North Carolina; they have been used for different reasons by Indigenous and Settler communities, scientists and managers. Evidence from 8,000+ years of human presence in the region challenges hegemonic narratives in which a uniform, universal era of fire exclusion occurred. Prescribed burning has been promoted as one of the best practices for restoring safer fire regimes and healthier ecosystems. Fire managers have been working towards increasing prescribed burning operations within their jurisdictions. Rather than centring a clear suppression versus burning dichotomy or simplifying variability, this article enlists the concept of ‘culture’ to smooth out the transitions between times when human fires were absent and present, and connects twenty-first-century institutionalised fire management activities to previous people’s practices. Intentional burning has strong causal effects in contemporary managers’ and scientists’ paradigms, leading them to integrate fire into multipronged strategies for managing the Nantahala and Pisgah National Forests.

title: ‘Stinking Hot Weather’: Embodying Fire Suppression on the Ground and in the Air in Mid-Twentieth-Century British Columbia
abstract: ABSTRACT Histories of aerial firefighting in British Columbia [BC]’s Forest Service often frame the mid-twentieth century as a time of transformation from an agency of patrolmen fighting fires with hand tools to a technological system governed by enlightened professionals. The aeroplane was a convenient commemorative shorthand for a classic story of technological progress and success in fire suppression. In this article, we listen closely to the oral histories of two forest rangers working on the fire line during the introduction of aerial fire suppression technologies in the mid-twentieth century. By analysing these interviews and related archival materials, we contribute to embodied and sensory histories of colonial fire suppression practices in BC and work to situate them in their specific institutional, social and cultural contexts. Close attention to the sensory experience of firefighting men shows how embodied, individual and situated knowledge shaped the work of fire control in the BC Forest Service.

title: New Research Project: Bodily Biographies of the Bronze Age
abstract: The newly funded research project, Bodily Biographies of the Bronze Age (BODYBIO), takes its point of departure from the intersection of the body, society and material culture in the Nordic Bronze Age (NBA, c. 1700–500 BCE). By combining theoretical perspectives from New Materialism with those of classical sociology, we use artefacts as proxies for fragmented and missing bodies. BODYBIO combines the study of these artefacts together with stateof- art osteological re-examination and scientific analysis of heavily fragmented cremated human remains to reconstruct bodily biographies.

title: Ministerial Power in Kantei-Led Policymaking: The Case of the Priority Reform Promotion System for National Universities under the Second Abe Administration
abstract: This article examines the policymaking process of the Priority Reform Promotion System, a performance-based funding system for Japanese national universities introduced under the second Abe administration. Existing research has largely portrayed this process through the lens of Kantei-led (prime minister’s office-led) policymaking, which sees the Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (MEXT) as following directives set by prime ministerial councils. However, little attention has been paid to whether and how MEXT’s own preferences were incorporated into the policy design. Using policy documents and elite interviews with MEXT civil servants, this article traces the policymaking process from agenda setting to the final budget negotiations, taking seriously the agency of MEXT. The findings show that MEXT held clear preferences from an early stage and shaped the design of the system within the new Kantei-led structure. These findings indicate that the Kantei-led framework does not on its own explain who determines specific policy content and suggest that ministerial agency deserves closer attention in analyses of Japan’s centralised policymaking structure.

title: Environment, Infrastructure and Epidemics in Late Ottoman Bursa: A Perspective from Environmental History
abstract: Examining epidemic diseases from the perspective of environmental history demonstrates that epidemics were not merely the result of biological processes, but were produced within socio-ecological interactions shaped by water infrastructures, industrial production, waste regimes, animal mobility and rural–urban circulation. By centring the concepts of environmental memory (continuity or rupture between past, present and future) and infrastructural inertia (inaction, stagnation, immutability and consequently deterioration and obsolescence), this study reveals that, despite administrative reforms, the risks associated with epidemics persisted through the material environment and deeply entrenched infrastructures. Through the case of Bursa, this article argues that epidemics cannot be understood independently from their environmental and infrastructural contexts. Archival documents and sanitary reports demonstrate that the structural deterioration of Bursa’s water distribution systems, the organic waste generated by silk production, the role of animal markets in zoonotic circulation and rural–urban mobility collectively shaped epidemic dynamics. Although modern public health measures such as quarantine and cordon practices were implemented, contaminated water flows, production-based waste, uncontrolled animal movements and livelihood-driven compulsory mobility limited the effectiveness of these measures. The study concludes that the effectiveness of public health policies …

title: Who cares about Otto? The monument of Otto von Bismarck in Bielefeld between commemoration, forgetting, and intervention
abstract: Monuments remain physically present long after the commemorative practices and shared interpretations that once sustained them have eroded. This article examines this process through the history of the Bismarck monument in Bielefeld, Germany, from its inauguration in 1903 to the present. Drawing on archival sources, newspaper reports, city council records, and documentation of recent interventions, it traces three successive memory regimes: national-heroic commemoration, postwar historicization and spatial marginalization, and the contemporary pluralization of meaning. It shows that political ruptures do not necessarily coincide with mnemonic change and that forgetting often unfolds gradually through shifting practices, spatial contexts, and communities of memory. Treating forgetting not as erasure but as a constitutive operation of memory, the article argues that the erosion of established meanings creates the conditions for new and competing historical appropriations.

title: A Technological and Ecological Tangle: Growers, Insects and Pesticides in Norwegian Horticulture, 1945–1960
abstract: The springboard for this article is a student diary from a Norwegian horticultural college in 1950. The notebook provides insights on how to use chemical insecticides, or in other words, poisons. The student kept day-to-day notes on what he was taught, and what he practised in the greenhouses and out in the fields and orchards. Alongside his fellow students in post-war Norway, he was taught to use toxic substances to ‘manage’ elements in nature. The diary is a snapshot of pesticide practices at that horticultural college from March to October 1950. After World War Two, efforts in horticulture to cultivate and control non-human nature, such as insects, intensified as new technologies such as industrial machines and different chemicals became readily available, firmly advocated and widely applied. These technologies facilitated changes on a scale previously unseen in human history. This article explores how new pesticide technologies affected the interaction between growers, plants and insects in Norwegian horticulture between 1945 and 1960. The investigation is based on the horticultural student diary from 1950 together with recently conducted oral history interviews from horticulturists who practised from the late 1940s onwards.

title: The Shifting Narrative of a Scottish Sandstorm in Time
abstract: This work explores the shifting narrative of the Culbin disaster, a series of storm events in 1694 that caused severe damage to a local community, with attention to the changes of that narrative over time. It highlights several major themes including how the human element of Culbin, despite being documented in the first accounts of the events, has come and gone from the narrative, the emphasis on the storm itself, the spiritual element of early modern disasters, the power of nature, Culbin as a symbol of triumph, and anxieties of climate change. Culbin serves as a long-term study of a disaster and explores how people chose to remember it.

title: Poetics as historical methodology
abstract: How can the tools of the poet enrich the writing of history? Some of history refuses translation. The past leaves gaping gestures in its records, for the historian to evade, or gloss over, or critically fabulate, as it leaves sediments of fractured story, layered through the processes of historical production. How can the historian attune to, and then amend, these formal contours of the archive? I argue that poetics can place the possibility and impossibility of recovering violent or entangled archives into the form of history-writing. I call for a re-envisioning of our forms of historical narration which draws from (or ‘Slants’) the poetics of the archive. Learning from four poets who embed the archive’s contours into the forms of their poetics, and from my own experiences writing archival poetry, I craft a poetics of history-telling that bares the seams of the historical process and holds those rhythms of the archive otherwise lost to historical prose. How completely can we embed the archive’s modes of memory-making into the form of our narratives? I turn to poetics as a new historical method.

title: The Catholics in the Aragalaya and the Aragalaya in the Catholic Church
abstract: Sri Lanka’s 2022 Aragalaya forced the Catholic Church to confront its own contradictions. As a fragile minority within a majoritarian ethno-state, the Church had long balanced prophetic witness against institutional self-preservation; the uprising broke that balance, demanding the Church ground its legitimacy in the justice it proclaims and answer for it. Within and outside the Church, the Aragalaya was itself an arc bending toward justice—yet one still anthropocentric and instrumentalist, its trajectory curving toward human ends alone, with little clarity about what justice ultimately demanded. This study argues that beneath this reckoning lies a deeper tension: a mandate for justice the Church cannot renounce, set against a complicity with its own dogmas and institutions it has not yet confronted. Even a Church awakened to human injustice risks repeating this same exclusionary logic at another register. What is needed, this study contends, is a theology of inclusive justice—termed here multispecies justice—in which justice is the inherent right of all species and their habitats, not a human privilege. Such a reckoning raises the defining question of an emancipatory faith: does the Church incarnate the freedom it preaches, or endorse that freedom in word while avoiding the cost of solidarity? For the Church to be in the world without being of it, yet confine its boundaries of justice to the interests of the nation-state, or shelter behind dogma and self-interest, is …

title: Spiritual Insights of Magnifica Humanitas
abstract: The article is an attempt to bring to light the least-explored dimension of the Encyclical Magnifica Humanitas, spirituality. The presentation is organised into six headings, excluding an introduction and a conclusion. Magnifica Humanitas argues that Humanity must place the God-given dignity of the human person at the centre of technological progress, ensuring that AI serves the common good rather than reducing people to measurable, exploitable datasets. The encyclical is a reminder that working towards social justice is a key part of our faith and Christian spirituality. The Incarnational Spirituality becomes clear in the closing paragraphs of Magnifica Humanitas and is present throughout the document. Pope strongly recommends establishing concrete criteria for discernment, which foremost include personal responsibility. The spirituality we need today is a Eucharistic spirituality, that is, a spirituality of ecclesial unity in love. Drawing on the encyclical’s title, the text highlights Mary as an icon of humble faith. It encourages individuals to become “weavers of hope” regardless of political or technological turmoil.

title: A View from the Italian Side: Transit Migrants from the Soviet Union in Italy during the 1970s and 1980s
abstract: Abstract During the 1970s and 1980s, thousands of migrants from the Soviet Union transited through Italian territory. Awaiting Western immigrant visas, people spent weeks or months in the maritime periphery of Rome. Based on Italian archival evidence, the article discusses how this migration was perceived in Italy. The article interprets the ex-Soviet transit as an integral part of the broader migrations that crossed Europe during the second half of the twentieth century. Within the Italian context, I inscribe the transit in the tectonic shift from emigration to immigration that Italy underwent from the 1970s onward. Scholars have commented on how slowly Italian government policies and legislation came to appreciate the country’s changing migration landscape. This article goes further by connecting high-level politics to the situation on the ground—in the localities where people from the Soviet Union stayed—and shows how ordinary Italians confronted the new migratory reality face to face. Although the former Soviet citizens were transit migrants rather than immigrants proper, the challenges they faced had much in common with those encountered by many immigrants from other countries. In that sense, the reception of the ex-Soviets not only revealed the extent to which Italian society was (un)prepared for these new population dynamics but also offered an instructive preview of the larger, more bitterly contested migrations that awaited Italy and the rest of the Western world.

title: BCOF at eighty: new perspectives on the British commonwealth occupation force in the occupation of Japan
abstract: The British Commonwealth Occupation Force (BCOF) component of the Allied Occupation of Japan (1945-1952) has often been overlooked by researchers because of its minimal role in policy-making. Taking the opportunity of the 80th anniversary of the arrival of the first BCOF personnel in Japan, this special issue introduces new perspectives about the organisation based on a range of hitherto unused or under-utilised sources. The introduction begins by emphasising how BCOF’s commanding officer sought to draw attention to his troops’ contribution to the Occupation. There follows a brief overview of the existing secondary research about BCOF in English and in Japanese. The latter half of the introduction outlines the contribution that the four articles make to the special issue. Taken as a whole, the purpose of the special issue is to begin to reassess how the occupiers and the occupied understood the role and meaning of BCOF. The introduction concludes with a call for other researchers to take part in the process of making this reassessment.

title: A FAIR-er digital archaeological ecosystem? Experiments in decolonial intervention
abstract: Abstract This article investigates how digital colonialism and coloniality of knowledge are reinforced within the digital information ecosystem of ‘Big Dig’ archaeological sites in the Middle East, using the Syrian site of Dura-Europos as a case study, and proposes a practical intervention model to address these asymmetries. The research uses a practice-led approach to map the fragmented digital landscape (databases, archives) related to Dura-Europos, identifying ‘microcolonialisms’ in metadata and shared infrastructure. It then details an ethically grounded, collaborative model that utilizes the multilingual Wikimedia/Wikidata ecosystem to co-curate a Linked Open Data (LOD) dataset and facilitate multilingual, cross-border collaboration with Syrian heritage professionals. The digital footprint of colonially entangled sites is fragmented and unconsciously reproduces linguistic and epistemic biases from the Global North, excluding local professionals and communities. The experimental intervention demonstrates that flexible, open-source LOD platforms can be leveraged to enable bottom-up metadata enrichment and provide a mechanism for rebalancing widely used interoperability resources (gazetteers, controlled vocabularies). This work provides an original practice-led model for decolonial intervention in digital archaeology. It shifts the focus from merely digitizing collections to actively revising the shared LOD infrastructure that drives global discoverability, specifically …

title: The Protection of Refusal: On Disavowal in the Indian Ocean
abstract: Lauren Benton reminds us that to write about piracy as historians (and anthropologists) is to engage in projects of “myth-making and myth-busting.” As she notes, pirates are either imagined as “colorful rogues…inherently anti-authoritarian actors who possessed a penchant for experimenting with alternative forms of political solidarity,” or they are depicted in a less renegade fashion, one that shows “their integration in established, if fluid, networks of patronage and power.” Instead of colorful outlaws, Benton (2014) argues that pirates are more akin to lawyers engaged in “legal posturing,” converting “booty into property.” As political actors, their politics are often far from revolutionary. Benton’s scholarship has been at the forefront of this latter school of myth-busting, and her work has been inspirational in rethinking the relationship between piracy, politics, and maritime space in order to tell a different kind of sea yarn. As she wrote in her 2005 CSSH essay, “[i]n my sea yarn, the oceans have a quality of lumpiness about them, pirates strain not to break the law, and international norms take shape not at Westphalia but at the edges of the Indian Ocean” (Benton 2005: 701–2).

title: Negotiating the Colonial Dilemma Through Science Fiction: Translating Jules Verne in Early Twentieth-Century Colonial Korea
abstract: Abstract This article examines the emergence of science fiction (SF) in early twentieth-century Korea by analyzing the first two Korean translations of Jules Verne—Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea (1907–8) and The Begum’s Fortune (1908). It argues that these relay translations, produced during the years between the Russo-Japanese War and formal Japanese annexation, reveal how Korean intellectuals navigated what the article terms the “colonial dilemma”: the challenge of rethinking national identity amid accelerated modernization and encroaching imperial domination. Rather than passively importing European SF, Korean translators actively reshaped the texts through genre relabeling, annotation, and selective adaptation, using them simultaneously as vehicles of scientific enlightenment and as tools for articulating Korea’s precarious place within global geopolitics. The article further contends that the early Korean use of the term “science fiction”—predating its standardization in the Anglophone world—calls for a reconsideration of global SF timelines and assumptions about the genre’s origins. By situating Korean SF within the broader East Asian circulation of Verne’s works and by highlighting the translators’ interventions into colonialist narratives, this study demonstrates that SF in Korea emerged not as an extension of European imperial imagination but through a complex interplay of colonial, anti-colonial, and nation-building impulses.

title: Archaeological Translation: How to Translate Diasporic Korean Literature
abstract: Abstract Min Jin Lee’s Pachinko chronicles four generations of Zainichi (Koreans in Japan) from the colonial era to the 1980s. Its translation process remains enigmatic; Lee imagined the narrative in Korean and Japanese before writing the novel in English. Consequently, the English original and its two Korean translated versions produce divergent meanings. This article investigates the translational issues in the two Korean versions, questioning the hierarchical order between the original Anglophone text and its translations. Building upon postcolonial translation scholarship, we first examine restored dialects in the Korean versions that are absent in the English text, analyzing their intersection with discourses of class, gender, and ethnicity. Second, we compare the opening sentences of the three versions, unearthing distinct insights into colonial and postcolonial histories embedded within each text. By unsettling conventional notions of originality, this comparative analysis introduces a new framework termed “archaeological translation.” Through this lens, we critique Lee’s mode of representation that flattens cultural and historical specificity, while demonstrating how translated versions evolve into distinctive texts with their own historical, political, and cultural perspectives in the transnational age.

title: Reading O Changhwan Translating Sergey Esenin in Seoul, 1946
abstract: Abstract This article explores the allegorical layers of meaning that emerge from one translator-poet partnership in the aftermath of the collapse of the Japanese empire in Korea. The iconoclastic modernist poet O Changhwan’s first published book in a newly liberated Korea was a translation of poems by the deceased Russian poet Sergey Esenin. O was translating at a moment when the Korean language was returning to public life after suppression under colonial rule and amid escalating violence on the partitioned peninsula. Reading O’s translations and lengthy afterword opens a window onto the scene of Seoul in 1946, one year before O was to cross over the thirty-eighth parallel into the northern zone. With the aim of rethinking the creative legacies of the early Cold War, this article explores the many meanings created in and through O’s translation.

title: 水野忠成政権期における知行割制度の運用実態 : 天保二～三年の秋田藩村替交渉における政務処理をめぐって
abstract: 老中首座松平信明の死去から天保改革開始に至る時期には、11代将軍徳川家斉（天保8年〔1837〕より大御所）の子女と縁組した続柄大名を中心とした一部の大名に拝借金の貸与や有利な所領替などが認められる不公平な幕政が展開し、幕藩関係に亀裂を生んだとされる。本稿では、この時期を「大御所時代」（家斉の将軍時代を含む）と称する。その中でも、文政元年（1818）に水野忠成が老中に就任し権力を掌握して以降、天保5年（1834）に死去するまでの17年間を、特に（水野）忠成政権期と区分する。忠成のような奥兼帯老中の場合、将軍の意志を伝達するとともにそれを執行する立場にあり、専制的な政権運営になりやすいとされる。そのため忠成は田沼意次と同視されることが多かった。 しかし、忠成政権期の幕政を正面から分析した研究は少ない。その中で概説書ではあるが、天保改革の前史として、大御所時代の政権構造を取り上げた藤田覚『水野忠邦』（東洋経済新報社、1994年）は、①拝借金の貸与、②所領替、③家格の引上げといった諸局面において「続柄」大名に対する露骨な優遇策が講じられ、その結果、全体として金権政治が横行し、他の大名の不満を誘発したことを指摘している。 このうち、実証研究が乏しいのは①・②であるが、①は財源、②は宛行地という原資を要することから、いずれも幕府財政に直接的な影響を及ぼす点に特徴を有する。とりわけ②は、①と異なり、その財政的影響が一過性にとどまらず、当該所領が復帰しない限り持続するため、のちの財政状況をも規定するものであった。大御所時代には、続柄大名に限定されず、贈賄により続柄以外の大名に対して優遇的所領替が実施された事例も確認され、当該期におけるその横行をもたらした構造的要因の解明が求められるのである。 しかし、その交渉の実態はほとんど不明で、前提となる幕府の知行割制度が把握されていないために、その制度下で幕府役人らが、どのような論理で公平性に欠く所領替を実現させたのかが未検討である。一方、筆者のこれまでの研究において、当該期には知行割の手続きや仕組みはすでに制度的確立をみており、老中や勘定奉行といえどもその規則を逸脱することは困難であったことが明らかとなっている（拙稿「知行割制度と村替をめぐる政治過程」『日本歴史』913、2024年など）。にもかかわらず、大御所時代における恣意的運用はいかにして行われたのか。すなわち、知行割制度下において優遇的所領替を可能にした論理を把握することにより、知行割の制度と運用の関係が問われるべきである。 そこで本稿では、天保2～3年にかけて秋田藩が対幕交渉を行った大沢郷村替一件を素材として、知行割制度下において、幕府役人が村替および村替方法の変更（物成詰から高替への転換）の妥当性をいかなる論理によって構築し、それを実現したのかを分析する。とりわけ、高替による村替を成立させた論理的根拠の具体相を検証する。これは、大御所時代の制度運用が幕末期の幕府財政に与えた影響の分析および天保改革期における知行割制改革の展開を論じるための基礎的作業としても位置づけられる。

title: 『述学斎日記』からみる倉石武四郎の蒐書活動とその学術的・社会的文脈 : 個人・国家が交差する学問実践と近代日中交流史の一断面
abstract: 本稿は、倉石武四郎（1897～1975）が1928年から1930年にかけて北京で行った在外研究員としての学術活動、とりわけ漢籍蒐集に焦点を当て、その実態と多層的意義を実証的に解明することを目的とする。主たる一次史料として、倉石自身が1930年1月から8月まで綴った『述学斎日記』を用い、当時の書籍購入の具体的方法、経済的基盤、師友や学術機関のための代行購入、さらには国家的文化事業への関与に至るまで、重層的な活動の全体像を描き出す。 第一に、倉石の蒐書活動は、当時の北京に存在した多様な書籍流通システム――書店への直接訪問、書店員による訪問販売、「封書」と呼ばれる独自の競売方式、遠方書店への郵送購入依頼など――を最大限に活用したものであり、その詳細な記録は、民国期北京の古書市場の構造と取引慣行を具体的に解明する貴重な手がかりとなる。特に「封書」の運用実態について体系的な描出を試みたのは管見の限り本稿が初めてである。 第二に、倉石の蒐書活動は、単なる個人の書誌学的趣味を超え、当時の日本の東洋学をめぐる制度的・政治的な状況と深く連動していた。倉石は京都帝国大学および東方文化学院京都研究所の現地代行人として、学術機関のための書籍購入に従事するとともに、師である内藤湖南や狩野直喜ら京都学派からの依頼による書籍の捜索・購入・書写も精力的に行っていた。すなわち倉石の活動は、個人の学問的意欲、学派の知的継承、国家的文化事業という三つの異なるベクトルが交差する場において展開された重層的な実践だったのである。 第三に、倉石の蒐書活動は、後の書誌学的事業として『旧京書影』の編纂へと結実している。この事業は、北平図書館が所蔵する宋元善本の書影を撮影後に解題を付したもので、戦乱による散逸前に同館善本コレクションの状態を伝える貴重な歴史的記録として高く評価される。 第四に、義和団事件の賠償金を財源とする東方文化事業の一環として実施された陶湘蔵書の購入と日本への移送という複雑な事業の実態を分析し、倉石の活動が学問と政治のはざまに位置づけられることを明らかにする。買収交渉の過程や搬出に際しての秘匿措置、さらには中国側の協力者の存在などを通じて、当時の日中関係の緊張の中での学術交流の困難さと、それに対する倉石の対応を浮き彫りにする。 以上の分析を通じて、倉石の蒐書活動が、個人の学問的基盤形成、京都学派の知的継承、国家的文化事業への関与、そして民国期北京の古書流通システムの解明という多角的な意義を有していたことを論証する。倉石の北京での在外研究は、中国現地の学問風土に浸り、その精髄としての文献を直接蒐集・会得することにより、一人の中国学者としての確固たる基盤を構築した時期であったと言える。そこで形成された「倉石文庫」のコレクションは、後の日本の中国学研究、特に清代考証学や中国語学研究の発展に寄与した貴重な資料的基盤となっている。

title: 近代における茶道の視覚化
abstract: 近代の茶道について、田中秀隆は近世には遊芸と見られていた茶道が近代に至り国民国家・日本を代表する芸術に昇華したこと、また依田徹は実用的な工芸品として扱われていた茶道具が美術品とされていったことを論じている。本稿は、以上を前提とした上で、これまで明示的に扱われていなかった「視覚化」について、流儀の茶道及び近代数寄者の茶道との関係で論じるものである。 茶道は本来、茶事において少人数が味覚を含む五感で味わい、かつ茶道具に加え、主客の身体的芸術としての点前や喫食・茶等の所作を相互に賞玩するものである。しかし、近代に編み出された大寄せの茶会では、席主は多数の茶客の所作を充分に賞玩することは事実上、難しく、茶客による席主の点前の一方的な賞玩という要素が圧倒的に強い。また、流儀の家元等による寺社での献茶も行われ、多数の門人や観衆が家元等の点前を「拝見する」ようになった。これらは明治時代以降、著増した大衆門人を参画させるには適当な茶道の形式であり、結果として多数の視線が席主や家元等の点前に一方的に注がれるという「点前の視覚化」が進展した。 他方、近代数寄者の茶道を見ると、例えば代表的な大寄せの茶会である大師会で茶席と関わりが無い形で古美術品が展観され、かつ呈・喫茶を行わない「茶席」も設けられた。また、鈍翁・益田孝の次世代の数寄者の間では点前や呈・喫茶を重要視しない茶事も行われた。これらにより、主客の身体的芸術を相互に賞玩するという性格は概して捨象され、茶客が亭・席主の茶道具を受動的に鑑賞する、という「茶道具の視覚化」が進展した。博物館や美術館でガラスケースに茶道具を収容し展観する、また美術書中に茶道具の写真を収録する、という究極的な形も誕生した。 以上の点前及び茶道具の視覚化の背景としては、明治政府による欧米諸国由来の視覚中心の美術概念の請来に伴い、日本社会でも「近代＝視覚の時代」というエピステーメーが定着し、茶道もこの影響から不可避であったことが考えられるであろう。
