title: Can automatic reading be close? On the implications of using a large language model to identify interactions between lighting and emotions in French literature, 1838–1928
abstract: Abstract This article evaluates whether a generic large language model (LLM) can be used to support literary scholarship by (1) identifying relevant passages and (2) producing explanations for those selections in response to a research question. We designed a workflow that combined semantic retrieval, vector search, and GPT-4o-based evaluation, and applied it to ninety novels set in Paris between 1838 and 1928, including works by Flaubert, Zola, Colette, and Proust, as well as lesser-known authors. Asked to identify passages in which artificial light played a role in the depiction of romantic or loving feelings, the model was relatively successful. Although it recovered only about 16 per cent of examples already located through manual reading, 56 per cent of the 506 additional passages it suggested were judged potentially valid in a scholar-evaluated sample. However, the model failed to generate explanations that would be convincing close readings. Critiquing the notion of ‘automatic close reading’, we apply our own close reading to the model’s imitations of close reading, and identify four recurrent shortcomings: (1) the problem of contemporary semantics being applied to a historical corpus, (2) a possible sentimentalist bias, (3) difficulty in detecting irony, and (4) misattribution of causality. We conclude that, if LLMs were to be trained for literary research, a model would need ‘knowledge’ of the whole text, extensive cultural and historical awareness, and training in …

title: ‘The best men of the expedition’: mapping local agents in Capelo and Ivens’ journey through Angola (1877–1880)
abstract: Abstract When debunking Serpa Pinto’s exaggerations about the perils encountered in Africa, Hermenegildo Capelo and Roberto Ivens strongly stated he had been accompanied by ‘the best men of the expedition’. But Serpa Pinto was not the only one who had company. An analysis of the two volumes of Capelo and Ivens’ From Benguella to the territory of Yacca reveals the duo was assisted by a vast network of local agents that included guides, porters, translators, and many other natives who contributed to the construction of scientific knowledge and the formation of the collections gathered during their journey. In this article, we use the network visualization software Gephi to map the relationships between the travellers and those mentioned in the travel book to demonstrate the importance of sociability to nineteenth-century scientific expeditions. While kept invisible for most of the historiography on these expeditions, the contributions of local agents have recently been the focus of work centred on circulation. With dedicated software, we can now visualize these networks, bringing into light the social nature of fieldwork.

title: Citizenship and autonomy: Bilateral labour migration governance and its discontents in Malawi, Mexico, and Spain, 1919–75
abstract: Abstract During the 1930s, the International Labour Organization sought to establish standards for bilateral labour migration agreements on separate but parallel colonial and nation-state tracks. I interrogate the ramifications of these discussions across the subsequent half-century, integrating global structural scales of analysis with migrants’ perspectives on the ground. First, I trace the concept of the ‘temporary migrant worker’ in the bilateral migration agreements signed in the 1930s to the 1960s between Spain and France; Nyasaland (later renewed by independent Malawi) and South Africa; and Mexico and United States. I then show how common post-war ideas and pressures led Mexico, Spain, and Nyasaland/Malawi to invest local authorities with substantial control over emigration and deprioritize migrants’ comfort and safety. Migrant-generated sources, notably letters, petitions, and oral histories, point to a resultant convergence of experience unanticipated by international policy discourses: migrants coming to perceive their own states as a primary barrier to progress, dignity, and autonomy.

title: Dancing ambassadors: The Indian republic’s global cultural project
abstract: Abstract Beginning in the 1950s, emerging from the British empire’s shadow, the Indian government helped dancers become globe-trotting, state-sponsored cultural ambassadors, projecting a vision of the young nation’s art as ancient, sophisticated, and spiritual. Asserting a ‘national culture’ (understood by the formerly colonized as essential to decolonization) involved its reconstitution, despite claims to civilizational continuity. This article reveals how dance became the natural candidate for global cultural projection, the ways in which the state allied with artists in this endeavour, and the conflicts this engendered between them. It offers insights into the state’s anxieties about the nation’s image globally, debates within civil society and between politicians about Indian culture, and the logic underlying how Indian dance was presented differently across the world. The global projection of culture and its reception abroad was part of the contested process of defining it at home. National culture took shape as it travelled the world.

title: Creating an “Ottoman Siberia”: Punitive Mobility and Imperial Governance in the Late Ottoman Empire
abstract: Abstract This article examines exile as a mode of punishment and governance in the late Ottoman Empire. Drawing on foreign ministry and diplomatic records, intergovernmental correspondence, and penal legislation, I argue that exile was part of an expansive and legally entrenched system of punitive mobility characterized by the forced movement of convicts. Against narratives that treat imprisonment as the defining mode of modern punishment, I show how the lines between exile and incarceration were blurred in law and practice across the Tanzimat (1839–1876) and Hamidian (1876–1909) eras. At the center of this analysis of attempts to expand the exile regime are proposals—inspired by Imperial Russia but consistent with Ottoman policies of internal deportation and settlement—to establish settler penal colonies in Yemen and Libya that would simultaneously purge the imperial interior of seditious subjects and develop frontier provinces through convict labor. In tracing the emergence and denouement of these plans for creating an “Ottoman Siberia,” the article explores how proposed convict settlement intersected with the pressures of managing Muslim refugees and migrants ( muhacirin ). While plans for both free and unfree settlement were shaped by overlapping spatial imaginaries and developmentalist logics, the article considers why migrants were prioritized. Recovering this history situates the Ottomans within global histories of convict transport that have been dominated by the …

title: Reading Ramie from Plant to Fabric
abstract: Abstract Focusing on ramie, a fiber plant widely grown in the history of Asia, and its illustrations (from plant to fabric) produced in Asia and Europe, this essay compares knowledge in historical imagery with twenty-first-century botanical knowledge to show how botanical artists and early observers understood this understudied yet important fiber plant. These drawings in many ways correlate with modern botanical knowledge, but they also differ in distinctive ways. How illustrators chose to represent the plant and the fiber extraction process indicates not only their perception of the plant and the industry but also their aims—scientific, political, and commercial—in producing the illustrations.

title: Parsing Middle High German: exploring cross-lingual NLP for treebank construction in low-resource historical languages
abstract: Abstract Building syntactically annotated corpora, such as treebanks, for historical languages is a challenging yet vital task in digital humanities, as it underpins linguistic analysis and facilitates a range of interdisciplinary research. However, the scarcity of annotated data and the need for extensive expertise in historical linguistics make this process particularly demanding. In this study, we explore the potential of cross-lingual natural language processing (NLP) techniques as a semiautomatic solution for treebank construction in low-resource historical languages. We use Middle High German (MHG) as a case study. Leveraging the linguistic continuity and structural similarities between MHG and Modern German (MG), we effectively utilize the extensive MG treebank resources to develop a constituency parsing system tailored for MHG. Specifically, to design a semiautomatic system that integrates automatic annotation with manual validation, we explore two cross-lingual transfer techniques: zero-shot transfer and delexicalization; the latter removes lexical information to focus on syntactic structure. In our experiments, we first train parsers on MG treebanks, and then transfer them to MHG using the two cross-lingual transfer techniques. The delexicalization method achieves a parsing performance of 67.3 per cent in terms of F1-score. This performance significantly surpasses the zero-shot cross-lingual method by a margin of 28.6 percentage points. These investigations …

title: PERIODIZING GEOLOGICALLY OUTWITH (AND WITHOUT?) THE ANTHROPOCENE: PASTS, AGENCIES, AND THE TERRESTRIAL
abstract: ABSTRACT As a periodization that is generally understood to refer to an era of Terrestrial relationships that developed with modernization and nuclearization, the Anthropocene cannot be applied simply to premodern histories and texts. However, it has introduced historians to geological periodization as a mode of describing periods of changed Terrestrial relationships in time. This article suggests that, in thinking about how historicizing texts conceptualized environments, geological (“‐ocene”) periodization provides a useful model and grammar by which to observe and describe how authors understood their environmental pasts, the agencies involved in reshaping Terrestrial regimes, and the role of environments in periodization. This article uses two genres of historicizing texts from Western Britain in the twelfth century to develop an approach to reading geological periods out of such texts. It suggests that doing so not only reveals important information about how these authors thought about environments in time but also provides a model by which the “geological turn” in the environmental humanities and premodern history can be put into mutually productive conversation without being inappropriately constrained by a term that was developed for modern phenomena. Outwith the Anthropocene, reading texts for what they say about environmental pasts, times, and agencies enables environmental thought to be analyzed in multiple dimensions.

title: ASSEMBLING PASTS, PROJECTING FUTURES: READING TINTIN WULIA'S A THOUSAND AND ONE MARTIAN NIGHTS WITH NANCY FLORIDA'S WRITING THE PAST, INSCRIBING THE FUTURE
abstract: ABSTRACT In Writing the Past, Inscribing the Future: History as Prophecy in Colonial Java , Nancy K. Florida identified a form of Javanese historical writing in which telling the past is a political act, one oriented to envisioning possible futures. This essay examines an experimental video by the artist Tintin Wulia that resonates with this prophetic form of history. Wulia's video, A Thousand and One Martian Nights , blends documentary and science fiction to tell the stories of political prisoners sent to the island of Buru as if they were exiles cast away to Mars in 2065. Footage from the United States’ space program in 1965 contributes to the futuristic tone while setting the decimation of the Indonesian leftist movement within the context of US imperialism. This layered video unsettles the conventions of historical evidence and linear narrative, eschewing conventional documentary forms that the New Order regime appropriated for state propaganda. Wulia's collaged historical text challenges the evidentiary claims that underpin conventional historiography and reimagines the past to open paths toward more just futures. By staging an unlikely dialogue between Wulia's video and Florida's reading of the Babad Jaka Tingkir , this essay aims to extend the efficacy of Florida's text. It argues that, however profoundly engaged it is with a specific literary tradition and historical context, Florida's text offers us generative ways to think broadly about the politics and potentials …

title: NOT QUITE A PROPHET FACING BACKWARD: ON HISTORY AS EXTENSION OF PROPHECY
abstract: ABSTRACT This essay develops the concept of history‐as‐extension‐of‐prophecy , a mode of historiographical reasoning that unsettles the dominant modern opposition between tradition as temporal continuity and revolution as temporal rupture. Through a close reading of Aḥmad b. ʿAbdallāh al‐Saqqāf's (1882–1950) Tārikh Sulṭanat Bāntan al‐Islamiyya , a mid‐twentieth‐century Arabic history of the Islamic Sultanate of Banten (West Java), I show how prophetic temporality operates as a form of historical extension, linking past, present, and future through an inherited script whose fulfillment remains open, deferred, and actionable. Drawing on Nancy K. Florida's account of Javanese “history‐as‐prophecy,” I demonstrate that al‐Saqqāf mobilized prophecy not as eschatological closure or antiquarian devotion but as a historiographic method that renders time morally legible and political generative. Through the concept of miṣdāq (extension), al‐Saqqāf aligned dispersed episodes of anticolonial resistance and Islamic revival with a prophetic ḥadīth about a continuously “victorious group,” thus reframing Indonesian history as an unfolding exegesis of Muḥammadan truth. I propose that history‐as‐extension‐of‐prophecy illuminates a distinctive temporal politics, one that carries inherited promises forward while activating unrealized possibilities in the present. It neither binds political life to a fixed past nor surrenders it to revolutionary novelty. Instead, it mediates continuity and …

title: JAKA TINGKIR: ANCESTOR, KING, SAINT—FRAMING A JAVANESE HERO IN A POPULAR SONG
abstract: ABSTRACT As Nancy K. Florida stated in Writing the Past, Inscribing the Future: History as Prophecy in Colonial Java , in the more dominant historical traditions, Jaka Tingkir is recalled as the founder of the Central Javanese kingdom of Pajang, an ascetic, an exile, and a brave warrior. Well‐known from chronicles such as babad texts and other storytelling genres, the figure of Jaka Tingkir has inspired artists to reinterpret his appearance and role in their own creations. In this essay, I discuss an early twenty‐first‐century song that, in part due to its reference to Jaka Tingkir, became wildly popular and extremely controversial. Focusing on dialogic encounters (a key concept in Florida's work), I explore how, in their responses to this song, religious leaders not only reiterated historical narratives and cultural practices but also put these into new contexts, creating new pasts while envisioning future aspirations.

title: What is UNRWA for? The contested purposes of refugee relief in Gaza, 1948–1950
abstract: Abstract In the midst of the crisis of displacement caused by the 1948 war for Palestine, the newly minted United Nations contracted with the (Quaker) American Friends Service Committee to provide aid to Palestinian refugees in Gaza. Over the next eighteen months, as AFSC workers participated in the institutionalization of new and modern forms of internationalist refugee assistance, many of them came to think that the real goal of this regime was not protection or succour but order, containment, and prolongation—a conclusion that informed the AFSC’s decision, in 1950, to withdraw its provision of aid and turn over its operations to the new United Nations Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA). This article explores this brief and apparently minor historical interregnum in Palestine’s refugee regime with an eye to the enormously consequential questions it raises: who built these modern refugee regimes, what did they actually do, and to what ends?

title: INTRODUCTION: REFLECTIONS ON HISTORY AS PROPHECY, CONTINUING THE CONVERSATION
abstract: ABSTRACT In this essay, I provide brief introductions to the notion of “prophetic” historiography that I developed in Writing the Past, Inscribing the Future: History as Prophecy in Colonial Java (1995) and to the five essays of this forum that were written in dialogue with it. I argue that “history as prophecy” forms a practice of writing in which the “prophetic historian” seizes hold of a moment of past potency to self‐consciously reinscribe it in the historian's present so that it may become a context for action in the futures of its readers. In my book, that argument is developed by means of a deeply textured reading of a unique nineteenth‐century narrative history of Java's fifteenth‐century transition to Islam, a nearly seven‐thousand‐line poetic history that was written by a royal exile. Each of the five essays engages my notion of “history as prophecy” in conversation, extending it into other realms of historical expression. The subjects of these five essays include contemporary performance cultures in Indonesia, an Arabic‐language Islamic history of the Indonesian past, genealogical practices of Acehnese Sufis, and Indonesian literary history.

title: TEMPORALITIES OF FREEDOM: DID NANCY FLORIDA'S BABAD JAKA TINGKIR “PROPHESY” MARCO KARTODIKROMO'S STUDENT HIDJO ?
abstract: ABSTRACT In her discussion of two episodes in the Babad Jaka Tingkir , a little‐known and incomplete nineteenth‐century Javanese narrative poem that is part genealogical history and part fictional romance, Nancy Florida asserted that these episodes, which are the two most “novelistic” episodes in the Jaka Tingkir “history,” hint at a new kind of historical writing. In this essay, I begin by interrogating what Florida meant when she called the Babad Jaka Tingkir “a historical prophecy” and then consider whether Student Hidjo (A Student Named Hijo), a 1918 novel written in Malay prose by a Javanese journalist and novelist, Marco Kartodikromo (1890–1932), can be interpreted as a fictional representation of what Florida termed “a new historiographic project” rather than as merely an interesting literary echo of a Javanese “history” written fifty years earlier in colonial Java.

title: REENCHANTMENT, INEFFABILITY, AND “THE DIALECTIC OF NOMINALISM”
abstract: ABSTRACT Martin Jay's newest book, Magical Nominalism: The Historical Event, Aesthetic Reenchantment, and the Photograph , aims to reveal the presence of a third current of thought in modern thinking. This current, which he calls “magical nominalism,” does not fit the traditional dichotomies (voluntarism–determinism, subjectivism–realism, and so on) around which the field's prevailing narratives are organized. As he shows, magical nominalism participates in the process of destroying the Scholastic idea of a perfectly ordered cosmos (an idea that was initiated by nominalism in the fourteenth century) but introduces into the nominalist matrix of thought a reference to an ontological dimension of reality that was initially absent from it. However, as he insists, magical nominalism does not constitute a homogeneous current. This form of thinking resists definition in unequivocal terms. Studying it therefore requires an approach that is capable of articulating a plurality of views.

title: Solar Photography
abstract: Abstract The mid-nineteenth century adoption of the new technology of photography transformed astronomical and meteorological practices. Today, there are upwards of ten million astronomical photographic negatives in observatory collections—a fraction of which are undergoing digitization to contribute to growing online databases of the astronomical archive, such as Germany’s Archives of Photographic Plates for Astronomical Use (APPLAUSE) and Digital Access to a Sky Century at Harvard (DASCH). As scientists revisit these images for time-domain astronomy, historians too are attuned to their significance to understanding the material conditions of their production. Focusing on a specific sunspot group, this essay situates these surviving plates in the visual and material cultures of astronomy and meteorology in the British colonies in the early twentieth century. It argues that such photographic plates, used in conjunction with more conventional documentary sources, can shed light on contemporary cultures of weather watching and forecasting.

title: Emerald Sea and Red Roofs
abstract: Abstract Red tile roofs are the icon of the Chinese coastal city, Qingdao, favored by German colonizers, Japanese invaders, and, most importantly, millions of Chinese who have resided in and built the city. This essay argues that, rather than treating them merely as cultural symbols, the red roofs, along with the cityscape they adorn, are a material artifact that blends both natural and cultural elements. They form a type of nature’s archive, recording the entangled environmental and cultural past of the city. We can learn to read and interpret these archives by analyzing our shared biological roots, the clay, the fuels, the tile-making process, the material sediments stored in the roofs, and the disposal process at the end of the tiles’ lifespan. By approaching the red roofs this way, they are no longer simply a German colonial heritage imposed on this Chinese city. On the contrary, we come to recognize a more complex history of the city, shaped by both external natural materials and our own inner desires and practical needs.

title: Cattle Censuses
abstract: Abstract Colonial historians have analyzed how human population censuses were instrumental for state-making and ethnic categorization, and how they can be used for demographical reconstruction. By contrast, they have thus far ignored the significance and analytical potential of livestock censuses. This essay teases out their potential for historical analysis by focusing on cattle censuses in French colonial Madagascar (1896–1960). It argues that colonial authorities went to great lengths to count cattle, deemed a key economic resource of the island, and showcase their numerical evolution in statistics, graphs, and maps. Due to context- and species-specific limitations of the data, historians cannot easily use these censuses to reconstruct cattle demography. Yet, they offer a fruitful lens to analyze cattle policies and knowledge regimes under colonial rule. Censuses were both an instrument of knowledge, used to monitor the evolution of the herds and reconceive policies, and an instrument of extraction, on which the annual cattle head tax was based. In both cases, cattle censuses were also sites of contestation. Tax extraction warranted strategies of dissimulation from the part of cattle owners, making knowledge even more unstable and causing epistemological anxieties within the colonial administration.

title: Resolving South Korea’s Dog Meat Conflict: Insights from Q Methodology
abstract: Abstract The consumption of dog meat in South Korea remains a contentious issue, fueling social conflict due to deeply held opposing views. This study employs Q methodology to identify diverse perspectives on dog meat consumption and derive strategies for conflict resolution. By examining the historical and cultural contexts and applying Q methodology with university students, the research highlights the need for a government-led collaborative governance model. This framework should integrate scientific evidence and public engagement to effectively manage the conflicting interests surrounding dog meat consumption.

title: Ghost elephants and the archive: Towards nonhuman histories beyond linear time
abstract: This paper examines a colonial-era memorial in Perak, British Malaya, commemorating a wild elephant killed in a collision with a train. Surviving archival records present a historical puzzle: a linear reading suggests the memorial likely conflates two separate elephant-train incidents in different times. The paper then asks what becomes visible when the same material is read through the Malay frontier's multi-temporal belief systems – one where the elephant is regarded as a richly temporal subject, a being whose significance could organise landscape and memory beyond its death. Drawing on pre-Islamic Malaya's syncretic belief systems and conceptions of time, chiefly the logic of kramat and the figure of the ghost elephant, the paper argues that the memorial's temporal disjuncture, rather than remaining contradictory, becomes historically coherent when read through this framework rather than linear historiography alone. Taking local logics seriously as a historiographical method can recover a historical intelligibility otherwise foreclosed – offering one approach to history that exceeds the empirical reach of the material archive.

title: Literary Expression at the Ends of Unicode
abstract: Abstract This article examines how Unicode reshapes the humanities by asking what happens when a supposedly universal encoding system meets the demands of the Japanese writing system. Focusing on EnJoe Toh's 2018 collection A Whirlpool of Glyphs, it shows how his fiction probes the tension between standardization and expression that underlies script reform from the Qin dynasty to contemporary Unicode debates. EnJoe's stories stage conflicts between inclusion and exclusion—what counts as an encodable character, which graphic forms are discarded, and how these decisions constrain or enable writers working with Sinographs, kana, and their visual and expressive possibilities. By dramatizing everything from Qin-era script reforms to rebellious furigana and proliferating variant characters, EnJoe makes visible the technical infrastructures that underwrite the process of writing. In doing so, the article argues, he exploits the Japanese writing system's capacity for orthographical variation at the limits of possibility. Unicode functions simultaneously as a tool of global standardization and a platform that “standardizes the nonstandard,” with significant consequences for how the humanities preserve, classify, and imagine written forms, and EnJoe's work offers a key case for understanding how script technologies condition literary creativity across languages and periods.

title: Reading Conflict Landscapes
abstract: Abstract Intervisual analysis, using Geographic Information Systems to compare historic satellite imagery with ground-sourced information and maps, offers new methods for analyzing changes in conflict landscapes over time. By pairing visual data with local studies, oral histories, and texts, one may better appreciate visual biases in imagery and reveal hidden landscapes and histories. Intervisual approaches demonstrate how modern conflict sites like Phu Bai airfield often overlap with more ancient conflict zones and their spatial footprints can linger long after hostilities have ended.

title: Ivory as Archive
abstract: Abstract This paper explores how historians might read ivory as an archive of environmental history. Using six figurines from Ming and Qing China held at the Eskenazi Museum of Art as a case study, it situates them within three histories: one of modern collecting; one of early modern production; and one that foregrounds elephants themselves. Ivory itself is a kind of archive. Biochemical signatures within it record key aspects of elephant lives, including their diet, lineage, and geographic origin. In the case of the Eskenazi figurines, these signatures showed that the collection derived from elephants from six different regions, two different continents, and two different eras. Connecting the elephants’ histories to human ones requires a participatory and omnivorous approach to environmental history: building partnerships with museums and citizen-historians, interpreting historical texts, and collaborating with scientists. The approach affords the opportunity to relate human histories to the history of life on Earth on the one hand, and to grow the community invested in environmental history on the other.

title: Displaced women, law and competing patriarchies in late Ottoman Serbia
abstract: Abstract Focusing on women who were displaced, unclaimed, or left without protection in the shifting legal order of early nineteenth-century Ottoman Serbia— runaway wives, enslaved and manumitted women, fugitives, and kidnapped girls —this article argues that the burdens of transition into the modern state were experienced most acutely by women who fell through the cracks of overlapping spatial and legal regimes of control. Despite their varied circumstances, women shared a structural problem: they had no pathway to legal personhood, no rights to return to or leave their homes, and no protection unless recognized within a patriarchal household. Their legal belonging remained tethered to household authority even as new centralizing political and legal orders took shape. In this unstable transitional period, patriarchy was distributed and enforced across competing scales and legal structures, including households, villages, Ottoman imperial institutions, and emerging Serbian state structures. Drawing on Serbian court and administrative records from the 1820s–30s, this article traces how various local and imperial officials negotiated these tensions, suggesting that transitional legal systems inscribed gendered asymmetries into modern practices of repatriation, citizenship, trafficking, and statelessness. The article contends that modern patriarchies emerged out of early modern household-based legal regimes and systems of village authority, and that modern forms of …

title: Institutionalization and Market Integration in the Archaic Greek Economy: Modelling Overseas Trade from the Distribution Pattern of Samian Transport Amphoras
abstract: Abstract This article advances the view that there was widespread institutionalization in the early Greek economy from the end of the eighth century bce. Challenging the widespread assumption that Mediterranean market integration crystallized much later and only by the end of the ‘archaic period’, agent-based modelling is used here alongside the archaeological distribution of Samian transport amphoras to demonstrate the coordination that must have existed between trade partners in shipping olive oil from one end of the Mediterranean to the other. ‘Brownian flow’ models of randomized drift fail to properly reproduce the amphora pattern, while a model based on a network of trade hubs stretching from the Black Sea to the shores of modern-day Spain provides a much more robust solution. These results shed light on the navigation of various environmental niches, on the lived experience of the sailors distributing products such as Samian olive oil, and most importantly suggest that the early Greek economy was more organized— and earlier, too —than we have previously suspected.

title: Between commerce and sanctity: Ottoman policies and international boundaries in the early modern Red Sea
abstract: Abstract This article examines the transformation of the Ottoman empire’s maritime boundary policies in the Red Sea during the early modern period. It focuses on the dual character of the Red Sea, as both a religious frontier safeguarding the Holy Cities and a strategic maritime corridor within global trade networks. Drawing on Ottoman and British archival sources, the study analyses the period from 1517 to 1798 in three distinct phases: a closed sea era shaped by the Portuguese threat (1517–1608); a phase of negotiation with friendly European actors (1608–36); and a period of controlled openness (1636–1798), in which limited access was granted to merchants recognised as müsteʾmin (protected foreigners). The article argues that Ottoman maritime sovereignty in the region was not exercised through absolute control, but through a flexible and negotiable mode of boundary management. This perspective offers a contribution to early modern debates on imperial border-making and sovereignty by revealing how empires balanced ideological commitments with economic pragmatism.

title: Archive of the Seven Spheres
abstract: Abstract: During the last decades of the eighteenth century, the Kingdom of Mysore in southern India became immersed in reading the stars to ascertain its fate in times of war against the British East India Company. Seeking to know the order of the universe and its influence on the Earth, advisors and astrologers in the court of Tipu Sultan, the nawab of Mysore, compiled a library of Persian and Arabic manuscripts on the planetary sciences of astronomy (ʿilm al-nujum) and astrology (ʿilm ahkam al-nujum), including original texts synthesizing Persianate and Sanskritic knowledge of the celestial sphere. In the pages of this planetary archive, the cosmos—comprised of the seven planets of Islamic astrology—was mirrored by the climes of the Earth. Through knowledge of the stars and their movements and the use of talismanic objects to mediate planetary influences, the kingdom could divine and shape its future. This essay introduces this archive of the astral sciences, and explores elements of its visual and material culture, to trace views of the Earth and its place in the cosmos from the eighteenth-century Deccan.

title: Reading Nature’s Archives
abstract: Abstract Recent changes in Earth’s climate and the rise of AI are driving a “planetary turn” in education and the humanities as traditional boundaries between history, technology, and natural processes dissolve. This text introduces a “planetary library” framework built on the idea that the world’s textual and material archives are inseparable. This History Lab forum demonstrates how the method is the argument, using scientific and other methods to interpret non-traditional archives such as ivory, whale bones, solar photos, and aerial imagery.

title: Seriously Chaotic
abstract: Abstract This paper examines ran nō 乱能, an unconventional kind of nō performance that features parody, role inversion, and improvisation in an otherwise solemn and formalized art form. While nō is grounded in ritual and religious themes, ran nō introduces humor through unorthodox casting and playful gags, often during festive occasions. Focusing on historical records and a case study of the 2009 Shukuga Ran Nō in Kyoto, where even sacred themes were treated with playful irreverence, this study traces the origins, evolution, and functions of ran nō . This paper argues that ran nō fosters cohesion among performers, amateurs, and audiences by allowing for a controlled moment of transgression that ultimately reaffirms the values and structure of the nō tradition.

title: The Origins of Bear-Baiting: Evidence from Medieval England and France
abstract: Abstract Bear-baiting, the act of setting dogs on tethered bears to fight, was an important social and economic activity in early modern England. It has been suggested that baiting was practiced in Western Europe during the Middle Ages, but the evidence for such claims has largely been restricted to images of bears in manuscript marginalia. For the first time, this article presents an interdisciplinary overview of the literary, archival, archaeological, and visual evidence for the development of bear-baiting in England and France from the 12th century onwards. Our combined analysis of bears in texts and high-status locations (castles, abbeys, and towns) reveal similar customs crossing social strata in England and Northern France. This research also demonstrates an increased visibility of the practice in England after the Norman Conquest, changing our understanding of the development of bear-baiting in medieval and early modern England.

title: Food Security, Nitrates Capitalism, and the Haber–Bosch Revolution
abstract: Abstract This article reinterprets the early history of the Haber–Bosch process of ammonia synthesis through the transnational development of synthetic nitrogen production at Ludwigshafen am Rhein and Billingham-on-Tees, County Durham. It argues that the nitrates revolution in the early twentieth century was not simply a technological breakthrough but a contested project linking industrial strategy, state power, and food security. Tracing the British government’s wartime construction and subsequent privatization of the Billingham plant, it shows how economic orthodoxy constrained efforts to sustain state-led industrial co-ordination, even as private firms pursued cartelized forms of governance. It situates the British and German chemical industries within a shared political economy, and reframes fertilizer production as central to the emergence of modern food politics and the international political economy, anticipating later debates over sovereignty, inequality, and environmental limits. Recovering these histories reveals food security as a foundational problem of industrial modernity, with nitrates capitalism shaped by decisions about the governance of national resources, scientific expertise, and global markets.

title: Stars, Kings, Pirates: The Nine Emperor Gods Festival and the Making of a Diasporic Religious Ecology in Postcolonial Southeast Asia
abstract: Abstract This article examines the Nine Emperor Gods Festival as a site of religious transformation among Chinese communities in Southeast Asia, offering a lens through which to theorize how migration, memory, and marginality reshape ritual life. While the festival originated in Qing-era China, it was reconfigured across the nineteenth and twentieth centuries through colonial labor migration, local ritual innovation, and the institutional life of overseas Chinese organizations. Adopting a longue durée perspective, we trace the shifting identities of the Nine Emperors, also known in the diaspora as the Nine Emperor Gods, and their mother, the Dipper Matriarch, alongside the transformation of the festival’s ritual structure. We propose the concept of diasporic religious ecology to theorize how Southeast Asian Chinese communities reconstituted religious authority outside East Asia. These communities invoked China as a cultural origin while simultaneously rejecting its political legitimacy. The Nine Emperor Gods, often recognized as exiles, martyrs, or liminal figures, mediated these tensions: their ritual features became metaphors for the diaspora’s tenuous but enduring relationship with China. By treating the festival not as evidence of survival but as a method of reckoning with displacement, this study positions religious transformation as a medium through which exile, rupture, and authority are not merely remembered but actively reconceptualized.

title: The birth of Golden Week: rival adaptations of School of Freedom and the postwar constitution of Japan
abstract: The introduction of new liberties in Japan’s post-war constitution sparked nationwide debate during the final years of the Allied Occupation. Shishi Bunroku’s satirical novel School of Freedom (1950) captured the public’s fascination – and puzzlement – over this influential yet elusive notion. Serialised in Japan’s leading newspaper, the Asahi Shinbun, the story follows a married couple navigating the social realities of early post-war life. The salaryman husband abruptly abandons both his job and his marriage in pursuit of freedom, prompting his wife to reconsider her own life prospects. Following the novel’s success, two film studios swiftly acquired the rights, and their competing adaptations were released simultaneously in May 1951, coinciding with a newly established string of national holidays. This timing boosted audience turnout, and the unexpected surge in box-office earnings led a film executive to coin the term ‘Golden Week’, which soon became synonymous with the holiday period itself. School of Freedom thus left an imprint not only on Japanese cinema but also on the cultural imagination and leisure practices of the emerging consumerist nation. This article explores the production and reception of the rival films, situating them within the late Occupation-era popular discourse surrounding the new rights – and accompanying obligations – stipulated by Japan’s 1947 constitution.

title: Working borders: Mad Studies, psychiatric museums, and decolonization
abstract: This essay considers recent, contemporary ’mad studies,’ in their activist, academic and museological dimensions, especially in the 2000s. It attends to mad histories in relation to Global North/Global South borders and other decolonizing aspects, and the emergence since the 1980s of mad/asylum museums in European and African manifestations. The notion of ’working borders’ is engaged in relation to disciplinary academic borders but also as working in scholarly or public elements and strands. It especially contextualizes such working of borders in activist historical work, thus beyond psychiatric historiography and since the 1960s.

title: Care as resistance and care as hope: ecocritical affect in Tawada Yōko’s The Emissary and Fernanda Trías’s Pink Slime
abstract: This paper explores how representations of nonhegemonic politics of care intersect with environmental degradation to reimagine human-nature relationships. Through transpacific comparative analysis of Tawada Yōko’s Kentōshi (The Emissary) and Fernanda Trías’s Mugre rosa (Pink Slime), I argue for comparative literature between Japan and Latin America as a decolonial methodology for Japanese Studies. My goal is twofold. First, I examine to what extent we can approach alternative modes of care as a way to understand the ongoing call to transform our relationships with the environment caused by the climate emergency. Second, I will argue how understanding this production in ways that defy the boundaries of area and discipline strives to put into practice an approach to Japanese studies that is organically decolonial. By integrating methodologies from transpacific comparative literature, ecocriticism, and ecofeminism, this paper contributes to ongoing efforts to decolonise Japanese Studies through expanded geographic and methodological frameworks.

title: Reassessing we : toward heterochronic histories of Japan
abstract: This paper analyzes the general exhibitions at the National Ainu Museum (NAM) and the Okinawa Prefectural Museum and Art Museum (Okimyū) to propose a new heterochronic approach to Japanese histories that deimperializes the present Yamato-centric narrative. Beginning in 1868, the fledgling Empire of Japan rushed to establish itself as a modern nation by, on the one hand, colonizing its neighboring regions beginning with Hokkaido and the residing Ainu population to the north and the southernmost islands occupied by Ryūkyū, and on the other, promoting its cultural sophistication through the newly compiled ‘Japanese art history’ that focused solely on the cultural production of the Yamato ‘Japanese’. Today, the imperial chronology at the core of Japanese art history and any other historical discourse of Japan continues to orchestrate a sense of unbroken progress and restricts ‘Japanese-ness’ in Japanese Studies to ethnic Yamato. Opened over ten years apart, NAM and Okimyū use different strategies to subvert the imperial monochrony of the mainstream Japanese history in their general exhibitions that transmit the heritage and identity of the communities they represent. By analyzing how the two institutions assert alternate conceptualizations of time through their gallery organization, this study argues for decentering and de-normalizing the present singular and linear imperial chronology as the first step to envisioning a deimperialized (and decolonized) Japanese Studies.

title: Embracing women: affective power and transformative empathy in Kirino Natsuo’s Daku onna and Murata Sayaka’s ‘Kakusei suru itami’
abstract: Kirino Natsuo’s novel Daku onna (Women who Embrace, 2015) follows its protagonist, Naoko, as she struggles to find her place within the student movement and women’s liberation movement (ūman ribu) during the early 1970s in Japan. This article also considers Murata Sayaka’s commentary on the novel, ‘Kakusei suru itami’ (‘Awakening Pain’, 2018), in which Murata claims to relate to and share Naoko’s pain. This paper argues that the pain of this historical moment—mediated through fiction—resonates affectively across generations, eliciting readers’ empathy and sharpening their sense of historical injustice towards women. Daku onna encourages readers to embrace Naoko’s subjectivity and plight alongside their own, while creating empathic linkages, or ‘coalitions’, between characters in the novel, and between readers and writers too. This article identifies narrative and contextual strategies that augment the novel’s affective power among Kirino’s readers. First, I analyse the novel’s paratextual, metatextual, and historical dimensions—including its title, cover, promotional discourse, narrative’s context—emphasising the significance of the events in 1972. I then draw on feminist theorisations of empathy as transformative to explore how textual features in Kirino’s novel and Murata’s essay invite readers to engage affectively with Naoko’s pains as a means of processing generational trauma. Finally, I reposition affective power and transformative empathy within a global perspective, …

title: Dead Bodies of the Okinawan Forest: Decolonial Subversion and Dangerous Nature in Medoruma Shun’s The Rainbow Bird
abstract: Post-war Okinawa has endured a complete reordering of its urban and natural spaces. The American administration expropriated lands from local communities for military bases, used Okinawa forests as storage facilities and training camps, and limited the local population’s access to significant places for remembrance and collective memories. This spatial reorganisation still stands today, even after Okinawa’s repatriation to Japan in 1972, foregrounding the importance of complex issues of land ownership and natural environment reclamation among Okinawan communities and external authorities. In his novel Niji no tori (The Rainbow Bird, 2006), Okinawan-born writer Medoruma Shun re-negotiates the position of the autochthonous environment and its non-human inhabitants within the Okinawan colonial establishment, decentring the human experience by proposing the forest as a complex actor whose agency impacts the colonial establishment. Through his writing, the Yanbaru forest emerges not only as a violently subversive site of decolonial contestation but also as an active character who works to resist the American colonizers and reclaim its independence from the Okinawan human community. By employing an ecocentric approach, this article broadens the discussion on the interrelation between the Okinawan forest and (non)human actors in Medoruma’s fiction, scrutinising how inter-species mediation as a base for deconstructing anthropocentrism in literary fiction can offer another path for …

title: Jeffrey S. Hardy. Finding God in the Gulag: A History of Christianity in the Soviet Penal System
abstract: In Finding God in the Gulag, Jeffrey S. Hardy tells the story of religious believers in the Soviet prison camp system. Although the Gulag—the system of forced labor camps in the Soviet Union—has been extensively researched, the story of religious faith in the Gulag is far less well known. Scholars have explored how faith and a sense of higher meaning and purpose helped people survive the dehumanizing environment of Nazi concentration camps. Although the history of Soviet atheism has received significant recent attention, the history of Soviet mass repression of religious believers has not. The Soviet regime did not simply disestablish the Russian Orthodox Church and institute atheist propaganda; it expended enormous effort to eradicate religion. Yet religion did not disappear: According to the suppressed 1937 census, over half of the Soviet population believed in God twenty years after the revolution, and the Soviets continued to battle against religious belief until the end. This book contributes to an important facet of that story.

title: Owen Robert Miller. The Conquest of the Mountains: State Violence, Technology, and Authoritarianism in the Ottoman East
abstract: The Conquest of the Mountains places particular emphasis on the Sasun massacre of 1893–1894 as a microhistory in the broader context of the Ottoman government’s protracted efforts to assert its modern statehood in the mountainous regions. Owen Robert Miller interprets this violent history as the history of the conquest of the mountains and places it in a larger history of “upland conquest, control, and colonization,” which he defines as a phenomenon encompassing the French campaigns in the Atlas Mountains, the Russian conquest of the Caucasus, and the British campaigns in the tribal areas (5). The book discusses the absence of mountains in general historiography, and dialogues with recent works on the history of violence in the Ottoman east. Ottoman strategy during the nineteenth century centered on the military’s efforts to eliminate the Kurdish power holders (mirs) in Eastern Anatolia, while cultivating new alliances with the less powerful Kurdish tribal heads as local intermediaries. The implementation of this policy in Sasun resulted in the imposition of double taxation, the perpetration of acts of plunder, and the continuation of violence by certain tribes against Armenian villages. The Armenian revolutionaries, specifically the Hnchak members, successfully organized self-defense units of peasants as networks in the Sasun mountains to counter Kurdish attacks. title: Ted Binnema. The Vancouver Island Treaties and the Evolving Principles of Indigenous Title
abstract: The principal goal of Ted Binnema’s The Vancouver Island Treaties and the Evolving Principles of Indigenous Title is simple: present a “disciplinarily historical perspective” on a series of fifteen land purchase agreements drawn up between 1850 and 1854 that are today known as the Vancouver Island Treaties (6). As the only such agreements between Indigenous communities and colonial authorities in British Columbia before the colony joined Canada in 1871, these “treaties” have occupied an outsized place in the complicated landscape of Canadian jurisprudence. Binnema argues, however, that the legal importance of these purchases has tainted modern examinations with “juridical preoccupations” and “other presentist concerns,” leading him to conclude that “the scholarly literature on the Vancouver Island treaties is badly flawed” (5). The thirteen chapters of this book present Binnema’s ambitious efforts to right this state of affairs. Chapters 1 to 7 delve into the deep history of these purchases, examining the land policies of the Hudson’s Bay Company (HBC) going back to its first trading expeditions in 1668 (chapters 1 and 2), the evolution of human societies on Vancouver Island since time immemorial (chapter 3), and the interactions between newcomers and Indigenous communities from the arrival of Spanish explorers in 1774 to the first purchase agreement in 1850 (chapters 4 and 5). title: Amazonian Storytelling as Co-Learning Within the Land of More-Than-Human Beings and Environmental History from Indigenous Perspectives
abstract: Oral histories draw on distinct traditions to narrate more-than-human worlds. In this article, we address their role in materializing the more-than-human perspectives and presences in the Amazon by focusing on the specific Apurinã narrative of Awãi, a story of one Apurinã ancestor. The analysis of Awãi’s story underscores the intimate presence and subjectivity of diverse more-than-human beings and their epistemological dimensions in oral histories. In Southwestern Amazonia, Apurinã stories are multisensory tools that have great power to communicate more-than-human social worlds and interconnectedness of beings. The story’s human and more-than-human characters are not from the past; rather, they are active subjects of the Apurinã social world and landscape. In the Amazon, the stories and storytelling moments play an important role in teaching both environmental history and environmental present shared with other sentient beings, as well as how to live and relate with them.

title: Radical accounting as method: interconnections across time, space, and bodies in Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater’s archives
abstract: This essay contributes to digital history by proposing ‘radical accounting’ as a method for gathering data from archives to support analysis of bodily practices at a scale that encompasses the transnational, intergenerational, and collective. Taking as our case study the Black-centered, multi-racial concert dance company Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater established in 1958, we manually curated data from over 30,000 print materials held by the Ailey Foundation, the Library of Congress, the New York Public Library for the Performing Arts, and the Black Archives of Mid-America, among others, to document all the artists who contributed to the company, all the dances that they made and performed, and all the places around the world where those performers and performances were seen. Through close analysis of datasets and experimental data visualizations, this essay demonstrates how radical accounting surfaces historical interconnections across performing arts ecosystems and artistic practices. While data ethics often emphasize incompleteness, radical accounting offers an alternative model for rigorous practices of care, drawing attention to the contributions of performers, contexts, and repertories relegated to the periphery of dominant historical narratives, and showing how embodied knowledge comes into being between and beyond all of these datapoints.

title: THE PHILOLOGY OF RACE IN LATE QING CHINA
abstract: ABSTRACT This article rethinks the problem of race from the late nineteenth century onward by examining how the concept of race configured an impasse in the relationship between history and nature in late Qing China. By analyzing the debate about race and history within late Qing philological discourse, it offers new readings of early foundational texts from China's long revolutionary twentieth century that address questions surrounding race, nation, and state. It takes late Qing intellectuals such as Zhang Taiyan, Liu Shipei, and Liang Qichao not as thinkers who were influenced by race but as thinkers of race—that is, individuals who scrutinized the coherence of a logic of race and its political possibilities. The fateful encounter between late Qing philology, the Kantian antinomy of race, and European comparative philology exposed the limits of a racial logic of reference by which the human was ordered on a global scale. This article locates within the reading and writing practices of late Qing philologists the demands on historical thought posed by a logic of race as well as its limits and contradictions. Thus, this article takes as its focus neither systems of racialization nor histories or genealogies of the concept of race. Rather, it scrutinizes the very use and coherence of race as a subject and/or object for historical thought. title: Surekha Davies. Humans: A Monstrous History
abstract: Surekha Davies declares that “[m]onsters are category problems that have to be defanged” (67) in her dazzling new book Humans: A Monstrous History. This politically engaged work shows how and why humans have “monstrified” other people across many different settings, deploying examples from histories of colonialism, gender, religion, science, and the environment in a deliberately wide-ranging work of accessible scholarship. Some of the most compelling and detailed examples come from the author’s background in the global history of the early modern period, but Davies adeptly juggles case studies ranging from the classical world to science fiction. She does so in order to ask the reader to assess the ethical implications of stereotyping others as “monstrous,” and to simultaneously argue for a positive, inclusive way of thinking about monstrosity through the lens of difference. These two strands are held in productive tension throughout the book. Davies’s aim is to build on the work of scholars like Saidiya Hartman: to engage with the challenges of foregrounding experiences too often lost (in Hartman’s phrase) to “the silence in the archive” (227). In practice, here, that often means empathetically centering stories of people who were exploited, condemned, or marginalized in their lifetimes for their perceived monstrosity. title: Robert Ivermee. Glorious Failure: The Forgotten History of French Imperialism in India
abstract: Scholars of French or Indian history (or indeed of European imperial or Indian Ocean history more broadly) might be puzzled by the book’s subtitle. They have not forgotten the history of French India. But Glorious Failure is not written for them. It is presumably a book written for the wider public, particularly in India and in France, which, as Robert Ivermee argues, have erased and forgotten this history, or worse, still believe in the myth of France “as a ‘good’ coloniser” (9). There are, of course, a whole host of studies about French India, but as the author points out, they are more focused or written in French, so this is an English-language book “chart[ing] the origins, development and ultimate failure of French imperialism in India from the late seventeenth to the early nineteenth century” (4). Works for public are often works of synthesis, and works of synthesis need to simplify. This monograph is not afraid to do so. Ivermee makes some bold statements (“the fiasco of American world leadership since 1945” [9]) and is clear in his own ambition: He wants to tell not only the story of intra-European conflict on the subcontinent, and that of French engagements with various Indian powers, but also to weave in the story of life in the French colonies, the negative impact of French rule, and particularly the persistence of slavery throughout the French Indian Ocean possessions. title: On the Place of “Meaning” in Traditional Festivals
abstract: Abstract In the literature about traditional festivals, the question of what the festival rites mean , or what they may have meant “originally,” is often at the forefront. Yet, in a fieldwork situation, festival actors tend to give seemingly random answers to such questions or make it clear that they are not relevant to them. On the other hand, festivals require constant investments of time and money, as well as access to public space, for which an explicit narrative of meaning is often necessary. What, then, is the place of meanings in festivals? This article uses the theoretical perspective of Humphrey and Laidlaw (1994) to analyze attributed meanings in the hanamatsuri festivals of Oku Mikawa, Japan. Tracing the history of narratives regarding the meaning of these festivals, I propose that while historical crises have at times called for radically new meanings, the development of festival performances has followed its own dynamic.

title: Confusion of Places
abstract: Abstract This article explores the concept of “escape ecologies”—landscapes whose physical and institutional illegibility allows people to evade coercion—by linking the present-day Białowieża Forest to eighteenth-century Eastern Europe. Based on field observations made during the state of emergency on the Polish-Belarusian border in 2021, this essay shows that modernized environments, including abandoned drainage ditches, collapsed spruce monocultures, and dense undergrowth caused by forestry practices, grazing bans, and climate stress might serve as effective corridors and shelters for migrants, despite the presence of drones, patrols, and fences. Juxtaposing these observations with early modern maps and administrative records reveals analogous mechanisms in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. In this context, unregulated rivers, wetlands, riparian forests, and river islands allowed deserters, fugitives, dissenters (e.g., Old Believers), and commoners to move about, hide, negotiate, and resist. Such a perspective challenges power-centric historiography, which overinterprets textual archives produced by rulers while undervaluing environmental archives and vernacular practices. Thinking through escape ecologies makes it possible to see why the poorly governed marshes and forests of Eastern Europe attracted fugitives, dissenters, and migrants alike—and why, despite the radically different technological conditions, they continue to do so.

title: Sarah E. Bond. Strike: Labor, Unions, and Resistance in the Roman Empire .
abstract: There is a long tradition of caution among Roman historians. Anachronism, modern terms, values, and frameworks can all easily overwhelm our fragmentary source base, creating false, overly modern interpretations. Our hesitancy has generated steady, but admittedly very slow, progress, especially on lesser-documented segments of the Roman population. We have struggled to effectively characterize, let alone categorize, some of these groups, as we seek to avoid importing baggage from other periods and fields of study. As Sarah Bond powerfully argues in Strike: Labor, Unions, and Resistance in the Roman Empire, we needn’t tie ourselves into knots to work on these portions of the populace. Anachronism, properly acknowledged and employed strategically, can be another tool in our kit, and it can be deployed to “return a voice of collective action to a conversation about labor in the ancient world” (5). Strike explores the power that existed within and was sometimes utilized by associations of workers in the Roman Republic and Empire. Bond begins in the near-mythological past of the city and guides the reader to the early Middle Ages in a comprehensive look at seven periods, each with distinct expressions of resistance from and attempts to control working people. The result is an accessible history of the Roman world that centers the experience of working people.

abstract: Reports of the violence in Warri in 1997 often got mired in the international condemnation of the execution of Ken Saro Wiwa in 1995 and news of the environmental devastation of the Niger Delta caused by petroleum. The Warri crisis over the creation of local governments was explained in terms of ethnic conflict: whether Olu, the Itsekiri monarch, was suzerain over a very heterogeneous region. Ethnic conflicts of this type were so commonplace that save for its widespread violence and devastation, the Warri crisis amounted to a blip and did not attract sustained national conversation or even much scholarly rationalization. In Minority Identities in Nigeria, Oghenetoja Okoh argues for the uniqueness of the Warri crisis even as it was set within a historically established pattern of political ethnicization by which the peoples of the Niger Delta were forged into colonial subjecthood and Nigerian citizenship. Scholarly disinterest, Okoh argues, is typical for a colonial and Nigerian historiography that considers minority populations as tangential to colonial purposes and to the structure of the postcolonial state. Yet, minorities have driven the most significant changes in Nigeria’s political history, both through efforts of the state to restrict their political participation and from how minorities have used their statuses to navigate adverse colonial and postcolonial exclusions. title: The Python God and the Empty Chair
abstract: Abstract This article explores how African royal power over the slave trade shaped transatlantic and cross-cultural interactions around sovereignty in the early eighteenth century. Employing an interdisciplinary approach, it analyzes the rich visual and material culture archive produced by the coronation ceremony of King Hufon of Hueda. This event offers a window into how Africans and Europeans negotiated, displayed, and subsequently reinterpreted cross-cultural relationships as part of competing political projects. By tracing the evolution of the story of Hufon’s coronation in Europe over many decades, the article shows how authors, artists, and publishers altered the memory and thus the archival imprint of Hufon’s power, obscuring the political subservience European merchants experienced in the kingdom. This formation of European imperial ideology occurred in parallel with a distinct but connected political process in West Africa, as the Dahomey kingdom overran and incorporated Hueda territory in response to the kingdom’s position within the Atlantic slave trade. The article argues that Hufon’s statecraft reverberated across African-European, inter-European, and inter-African relationships, demonstrating that the deep reconstruction of actual African-European relations in West Africa is necessary for understanding both Hufon’s coronation ceremony and how African power projected through Atlantic commerce shaped European and African imperialism.

title: Karin Wulf. Lineage: Genealogy and the Power of Connection in Early America
abstract: For far too long, the history of the family has been relegated to a secondary field of interest or even an area for genealogists rather than professional historians. In Karin Wulf’s adept hands, however, family history is essential for unpacking key historical questions about power, race, law, and gender. Lineage: ­­Genealogy and the Power of Connection in Early America offers a multi-layered, sweeping study of the way ­­eighteenth-century Americans deployed family histories as tools of governance and hierarchy. This richly illustrated, meticulously researched and argued book weaves together the latest innovations in cultural history to read a wide range of “texts.” Wulf’s voluminous source base ranges from a silver plate engraved with a family story to illustrated bibles to mere scraps of paper in archives across the eastern United States and England. Her mastery of the scholarship of “vast early America” (a term Wulf herself coined) allows her to contextualize her evidence in historiographies of family, law, religion, material culture, sexuality, and slavery. While this is primarily an Anglo-American story, Wulf situates the work in conversation with scholarship on the broader Atlantic world in this era.

title: Forever in Fiction
abstract: Abstract Against a backdrop of ongoing harm, this essay interrogates the limits of closure—in grief, nuclear decommissioning, and academic scholarship. I draw from an unexpected moment in my research on the Three Mile Island nuclear power plant’s sixty-year closure in which I discovered part of my personal history at the public library that caused me to reexamine how closure and containment operate in both the oral histories that people told me, and the academic training that calls for me to construct a tidy narrative from them. I compare this narrative form of closure in oral histories with the plant’s more subtle impact on everyday life, as well as my own endeavor to frame these fragments in ways that do not sacrifice their incoherence for a logical retelling of them. This essay challenges closure as a useful concept or method not only for nuclear decommissioning and grief but also for scholarship, and proposes the politics of resisting closure, particularly in the climate of late industrialism and capitalism.

title: Mining the Virgin Mountain
abstract: Abstract This article examines how the earth has been personified as female in colonial, extractivist contexts, focusing on the Andean mining city of Potosí, the wresting of whose silver was pivotal for the emergence of global capitalism. Specifically, it attends to La Virgen del Cerro (The Virgin of the Mountain), a painting by an unknown artist working in the eighteenth-century Spanish Viceroyalty of Peru. It depicts the mineshaft-riven mountain above Potosí as the Virgin Mary, her hands and head superimposed onto its slopes. Whereas Carolyn Merchant has argued that feminizing apprehensions of nature constrain resource extraction, La Virgen del Cerro sanctified colonial silver mining. By transposing Mary’s “postpartum virginity” onto the Andean environment, the picture melds two usually distinct colonial tropes: nature as an alluring virgin and a nurturing mother. The earth becomes an inviting female body, gestating resources for imperial consumption. Reflecting on the globe depicted in the foreground, the article argues that this maternal earth is incubating global capitalism itself, whose emergence the painting envisions as nothing less than a holy birth.

title: Contested Belonging
abstract: Abstract This article examines how local chiefs frame their relationships with communities and Mount Mabo through kinship, exoteric knowledge, and spiritual power in the context of growing impositions of neoliberal nature governance. The article shows that the amwene (local chiefs) hold authority due to their spiritual connection with what they consider sibling landscapes: the oldest brother, Mount Mabo; the middle sister, River Múgue; and the youngest brother, Mount Muriba. This allows them to control access to landscapes that NGOs and conservationists aim to protect. The article argues that by understanding the amwene’s cosmologies, a relational ecology emerges where mountains, rivers, and forests are seen as inhabited by the original local chiefs’ spirits that in turn mediate social relations and mutual belonging with the living chiefs and landscapes. This cosmology offers a powerful critique of neoliberal nature governance, which thingifies nature while exacerbating the separation of nature from society. However, more than providing an academic critique of neoliberal nature conservation in Mozambique, this article aims to offer valuable insights for reimagining conservation efforts in a manner that respects and preserves the integrity of both human and nonhuman worlds in the Anthropocene.

title: The Great River Speaks
abstract: Abstract This article examines the Mississippi River as an agent of communication and a form of elemental media in the context of medianaturecultures, suggesting a shift away from human-centric communication models. Drawing on Rosi Braidotti’s posthumanities concept, it suggests that understanding rivers as communicative entities challenges anthropocentric perspectives. The article especially focuses on the history of hydrological interventions and engineering, particularly river laboratories, which were a response to the river, as Mark Twain put it, “always moving bodily sideways.” These efforts, often contrasting hands-on approaches with theoretical models, especially in their initial phase, emphasized the river’s elusive qualities that constitute the complexity of its behavior. This, in turn, is mirrored by its discursive instability, including the attempts at defining the river. The article proposes that it is precisely such instability that can be seen as more-than-human communicative and material agency. Therefore, a parallel is drawn between documentation of early engineering endeavors and ontoepistemologies drawing from Indigenous traditions and concepts, such as Vanessa Watts’s idea of Place-Thought.

title: A Frog’s Anthropocene Story
abstract: Abstract Lin Zhao’s 2022 Chinese novel Chao Xi Tu (Tidal Atlas) is renowned for its unique use of vernacular southern Chinese dialects, recounted by its nonhuman protagonist Wa, a giant female frog. Through the lens of an ecofeminist reading of the novel informed by delta anthropology and migrant ecologies, this article analyzes the multifaceted amphibiousness and multispecies worlding of the Pearl River Delta in southern China in the early nineteenth century. The novel constructs a more-than-human histography through bold speculation set at the height of Western colonialism—a period that swept southern China into the material flows and displacements of the imperial-capitalistic-Anthropocene. As one of the world’s largest and fastest-growing urban regions, the Pearl River Delta has been dominantly framed as China’s past “World Factory” and present “Greater Bay Area.” Such territorialized and developmentalist narratives, however, have overshadowed the delta’s liquid geography, hybrid cultural identities, and fluid cosmologies. This article argues that Lin’s novel provides a timely literary reworlding of the delta and its amphibious, more-than-human materialities, while mounting a powerful critique of Anthropocene violence, a force that continues to extract from and marginalize both the delta’s amphibious matter and its forms of knowledge.

title: Ways of Listening, Ecological Sensibility, and the Ethics of Attention
abstract: Abstract This article argues that listening enlarges ecological sensibility, because attention to the meaning of nonhuman animal communication broadens and expands sonic awareness of place. The work of Aldo Leopold and Baptiste Morizot demonstrates how listening can weave together the deep time scales of evolutionary change and the immediate, affective dimension of embodied encounters with the sounds of animal voices. This way of listening becomes ethical and political when the ecological crisis is understood to be in part a crisis of sensory extinction, following the work of biologist David Haskell. The article demonstrates how attention is the necessary condition of ethical deliberation, engaging with the conception of attention put forth by Iris Murdoch, and argues that listening therefore has a special role to play in rejuvenating an environmental ethic of attention. Through a close reading of the chapter “Marshland Elegies” from A Sand County Almanac the article argues that Leopold understood how land health was intimately connected to the soundscape of place. Then the article considers how Morizot’s encounter with wolf howls and song deepens the meaning of attentive environmental listening. The article concludes by narrating a chance meeting with a barred owl from the author’s life.

title: Bewilderment
abstract: Abstract During the Romantic period, cathartic expressions of eco-anxiety resulted in a collective effort to evoke change through an influential wave of art, literature, music, science, and philosophy that spread across Europe, North America, and beyond. Due to the similar sense of loss and uncertainty that accompanies today’s rapidly changing climate, Romantic voices and ideals continue to be called upon to highlight the vital connection between humans and nature. A rising generation of writers, poets, artists, researchers, and activists across the globe, however, seeks to inspire affirmative climate action while acknowledging and making space for the hidden places, the excluded voices, and the forgotten stories overshadowed by Western Romanticism. This article therefore suggests there is an emerging movement of Romanticism guided by feelings of bewilderment defined in two ways: as isolation, expressing the uncertainty and unfamiliarity accompanying contemporary eco-anxiety; and as attunement, embracing the uncanniness of the Anthropocene by becoming more attentive to non-Western worldviews, deep time perspectives, multispecies encounters, and nonhuman presences. The featured literary and artistic interventions reveal how Anthropocene bewilderment can be harnessed to accessibly translate the ecological data dump, elevate underrepresented voices, and create new pathways for affirmative climate action and more-than-human planetary care.

title: Interpretive computing: designing for interactions between people, AI, and cultural heritage collections
abstract: Abstract This article introduces interpretive computing, a humanistic design framework for artificial intelligence systems that support collaborative meaning-making, narrative construction, and cultural responsiveness in archival contexts. Moving beyond explainability and automation, interpretive computing positions AI as a scaffold for situated interpretation—one that centres context, dialogue, and plural epistemologies. We develop this concept through a case study involving the Smithsonian Institution and U.S. Library of Congress Civil Rights History Project—oral history collection, where large language models are used to generate thematic metadata, segment interviews, and construct dynamic, user-curated story paths. Our prototype interface features include editable metadata annotations and thematic playlists, allowing users—whether educators, students, or community members—to engage in co-authorship of historical understanding. Grounded in traditions from hermeneutics, narratology, and digital humanities, this work reimagines metadata and interface design as interpretive acts, offering a model for AI systems that support dialogic, reflexive, and culturally situated engagements with the past.

title: An Absent Mother between Two States
abstract: Abstract Motherhood—one of the most important and yet mundane social institutions—is central to understanding the rise and decline of Third World internationalism. This article focuses on Francisca Casparina Fanggidaej (1925–2013), a left-wing Indonesian activist in the Afro-Asian solidarity movements that developed out of the Bandung Conference. She is also a mother of seven who endured decades of forced separation from her family. Based on a close reading of Fanggidaej’s diaries, personal letters, and oral history interviews with her family and friends, I discuss the politics of maternal absence in Indonesia and China—two of the leading countries in the Afro-Asian movements. I explore how these two countries shaped the public and self-perceptions of nonresidential mothers through their welfare provisions and reproductive policies. Against this backdrop, I examine how a transnational figure like Fanggidaej navigated motherhood within frameworks of revolutionary anticolonialism in Indonesia, state socialism in China, and the global rise of capitalist neoliberalism, which ultimately displaced the Third World internationalist vision once championed by both nations. title: Shulamit Volkov. Germany through Jewish Eyes: A History from the Eighteenth Century to the Present
abstract: Since the beginning of “modernity,” Jews have repeatedly been an object of inquiry by non-Jews who evaluated and disparaged their subjects’ religion and lives. The sheer volume of ink spilled on discussing Jewish emancipation and Jewish rights during the long nineteenth century (and beyond) demonstrates how central Jewish lives and religion were to self-definitions of Germanness; however, the writing of German history has struggled mightily to incorporate Jewish lives in anything but a peripheral manner—right up to the present. Often, Jewish lives—if they are presented at all—revolve around suffering, discrimination, and the Holocaust. Furthermore, the view from the historians of German history rarely reflects the views of German Jews and the times, places, and spaces in which they lived. The field of German-Jewish history has thus flourished where German history has lagged behind, and such scholarship has provided a lens through which we can view how Jews lived in the German states and in the context of the events of their time. Yet these historiographical traditions are in an asymmetrical relationship—the latter relies explicitly on the former, but the former can pick and choose when, where, and how to incorporate the latter.
